Frankenstein Transformer:
Unified Encoder-Decoder Library, CLI, and Research-Grounded Design Notes

Erick F. Merino M.
This work is not affiliated
erickfmm@gmail.com

October 2026

Abstract

Transformer architectures dominate sequence modeling across natural language processing, computer vision, speech, and computational biology, but the design space around them has fragmented. Attention has diversified beyond dense softmax into recurrent and retentive blocks, sparse patterns, gated mechanisms, latent projections, memory-augmented layers, and fast-weight rules; optimizers have expanded beyond AdamW with variance-reduction, memory-efficient, schedule-free, second-order, and low-rank methods. Comparing these ideas under consistent conditions remains costly, because each variant must be implemented, wired into a training pipeline, and maintained separately—a duplication of effort that hinders reproducibility and makes published comparisons difficult to align. We present Frankenstein Transformer, a configuration-driven CLI toolkit (frankenstein-transformer) that unifies model definition, training, deployment, and inference behind a single strict YAML schema. The toolkit covers forty-seven sequence mixers across ten families and twenty-four optimizer families with per-parameter-group hyperparameter control, and supports encoder, decoder, Vision Transformer and audio model classes for masked language modeling, causal language modeling, sentence embeddings, image tasks, speech recognition and audio classification. Its contribution is a validated experimentation contract: invalid configurations fail before training starts, every architecture and optimizer shares one operational interface, and the same document drives training, quantized deployment and export, and a schema-generated web builder. The contract is exercised end-to-end in a measurement campaign of 868 configurations (905 CPU-hours) that trains, exports, quantizes, and evaluates every mixer pair, optimizer, and deployment path through the same interface, published as an interactive report with downloadable datasets. We describe the architecture taxonomy, optimizer routing, deployment paths, and integration surface, and defer mathematical and implementation detail to the appendices.

Introduction

Motivation and Problem Statement

Transformer architectures are the dominant paradigm for sequence modeling in natural language processing , computer vision, and computational biology, with models such as BERT and GPT establishing the standard for representation learning. The field has since diversified rapidly: recurrent and retentive blocks, sparse attention, gated mechanisms, latent projections, memory-augmented layers, fast-weight rules, and continuous-depth formulations each address a different limitation of dense attention, while the optimizer landscape has expanded beyond AdamW with variance-reduction, memory-efficient, schedule-free, second-order, and low-rank methods .

The practical consequence is a fragmented ecosystem. Comparing sequence mixers or optimizers under identical training conditions requires re-implementing each variant, wiring it into a training pipeline, and maintaining the result across framework changes. This effort hinders reproducibility, slows scientific progress, and raises the barrier to entry for new researchers.

Proposal and Contributions

We propose Frankenstein Transformer (https://github.com/erickfmm/frankenstein-transformer), a configuration-driven toolkit that treats architecture, optimizer, and training choices as a single validated document. The project provides:

  1. Schema-first design: a strict YAML contract supporting forty-seven sequence mixers across ten families and twenty-four optimizer families, enforced before training begins.

  2. Architecture-agnostic training: one pipeline for dense baselines, recurrent and retentive blocks, sparse patterns, gated mechanisms, latent compression, conditional memory, fast-weight attention, and geometric-field attention, with encoder and decoder modes .

  3. Optimizer routing: prefixed hyperparameter groups that control embeddings, normalization layers, attention blocks, and remaining parameters independently for each optimizer family .

  4. End-to-end workflows: training (including sentence-embedding objectives), deployment and export (quantized, standard, HuggingFace Transformers, and BitNet GGUF formats), inference, and a schema-driven web builder inspired by SBERT-style workflows .

  5. Vision support: a Vision Transformer model class covering masked patch prediction, classification, and segmentation under the same mixer and optimizer infrastructure.

  6. Validation tooling: unit tests, YAML preset validation, and continuous integration across supported Python versions.

The command surface is frankenstein-transformer, with four subcommands: train, deploy, infer, and web-server. The last launches a Streamlit configuration builder that renders schema metadata as forms, validates input live, previews the resulting YAML, and generates the equivalent CLI command, serving both as a configuration aid and as documentation of the available design space.

Reading Guide

This document is organized as a technical reference:

  1. Prerequisites: Appendix 12 introduces transformers and attention for readers new to the field.

  2. Configuration contract: Section 3.1 describes the schema and Section 3.2 its validation rules.

  3. Architecture selection: Section 4.1 compares sequence-mixer families; Appendices 16, 17, 18, and 19 collect the supporting literature, with normalization, BitNet, and conditional-memory details in Appendix 20 and manifold-constrained residuals in Appendix 22.

  4. Optimization: Section 5 summarizes optimizer routing; Appendix 15 provides the full family analysis.

  5. Deployment and inference: Sections 6 and 7 cover quantized deployment and sentence embeddings.

Related Work

This work sits at the intersection of deep learning frameworks, training tooling, and configuration-driven experimentation. While Sections 4.1 and 5 survey the architectural and optimization literature in depth, this section focuses on the software ecosystem for building, training, and configuring transformer models.

Base Deep Learning Frameworks

The modern transformer research ecosystem rests on several foundational frameworks that provide automatic differentiation, GPU acceleration, and high-level model-building APIs.

PyTorch has become the dominant framework for transformer research. Its imperative programming model and dynamic computation graphs enable flexible debugging and rapid prototyping of novel architectures. The torch.nn.Module abstraction, automatic mixed-precision training via torch.cuda.amp, and the torch.compile JIT compiler form the backbone of most contemporary transformer implementations. Frankenstein Transformer is built entirely on PyTorch, leveraging its module system for composable architecture definitions.

TensorFlow pioneered production-oriented deep learning with its static computation graph paradigm and the Keras high-level API. While its influence in transformer research has waned relative to PyTorch, TensorFlow’s serving infrastructure (TF Serving, TF Lite) and the tensorflow-text library remain relevant for deployment scenarios.

JAX offers a functional programming model built around composable transformations (jit, vmap, grad) and XLA compilation. Its design enables clean implementations of complex algorithms and has been adopted by several recent transformer libraries (e.g., Flax, Haiku). JAX’s stateless design and automatic vectorization are particularly well-suited for research on novel attention mechanisms and optimization algorithms.

scikit-learn provides classical machine learning algorithms and utilities (preprocessing, metrics, model selection) that serve as baselines and complementary tools in transformer workflows. While not designed for deep learning, its consistent API and extensive documentation make it a standard reference point for comparing transformer-based approaches against traditional methods.

Out-of-the-Box Training Frameworks

Several libraries provide complete training pipelines that abstract away the complexity of distributed training, data loading, and hyperparameter management.

Hugging Face Transformers is the de facto standard for accessing, fine-tuning, and sharing pretrained transformer models. Its Trainer API, model hub with over 500,000 models, and tight integration with the datasets and tokenizers libraries have made it the primary entry point for transformer-based NLP. However, its architecture is optimized for fine-tuning existing pretrained models rather than experimenting with novel sequence mixer designs or training from scratch with custom optimization strategies.

Oumi (https://github.com/oumi-ai/oumi, 2025) is an open-source end-to-end platform for training, fine-tuning, evaluating, and deploying foundation models. It provides a unified interface across multiple cloud providers and supports both supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization (DPO, RLHF). Oumi emphasizes production readiness with built-in monitoring, checkpointing, and deployment tooling.

LLaMA Factory (https://github.com/hiyouga/LLaMA-Factory, 2024) offers a unified framework for efficient fine-tuning of over 100 large language models. It provides both a web-based UI and a CLI, supporting LoRA, QLoRA, full-parameter fine-tuning, and various alignment techniques. Its focus is on adapting existing pretrained LLMs to downstream tasks rather than architectural experimentation.

Axolotl (https://github.com/axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl, 2024) is a streamlined fine-tuning tool supporting LoRA, QLoRA, DeepSpeed, and FSDP. It emphasizes configuration-driven workflows via YAML files and has become popular in the open-source LLM fine-tuning community. Like LLaMA Factory, it targets fine-tuning of pretrained models rather than training novel architectures from scratch.

Low-Code and Efficiency-Oriented Tools

A growing category of tools prioritizes accessibility and computational efficiency, lowering the barrier to transformer training.

Unsloth (https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth, 2024) provides low-code fine-tuning with 2–5\(\times\) speedup and significantly reduced VRAM requirements through hand-written CUDA kernels and optimized Triton operations. It supports GGUF export for quantized deployment and integrates with the Hugging Face ecosystem. Unsloth’s focus is on making fine-tuning faster and more memory-efficient, not on architectural exploration.

dashAI (https://github.com/DashAISoftware/dashAI, v0.9.7.post2, 2026) is an open-source, local-first desktop workbench for machine learning developed by a Chilean academic consortium (Universidad de Chile/FCFM, CENIA, IMFD, and ANID funding). Its interface is fully schema-driven: configuration forms are generated directly from Pydantic component schemas with no hand-written frontend code, and its catalog spans roughly 76 multitask models—tabular classifiers, NLP models, translation, open-weight LLMs, and text-to-image generation—unified behind a dozen typed base abstractions. Extensibility is central to its design: plugins are ordinary PyPI packages discovered through the dashai.plugins entry-points group and installable from the UI, a mechanism comprehensive enough that even dashAI’s own generative capabilities (e.g., Stable Diffusion, Flux) are distributed as plugins. Where earlier releases targeted classical ML workflows, the current platform spans predictive and generative modeling across domains, making it a natural host for transformer components via its plugin system; Section 8 presents the dashai-frankenstein adapter built on this mechanism.

Configuration-Driven Experimentation

A common thread across the tools surveyed above is their focus on fine-tuning existing pretrained models. Hugging Face Transformers, LLaMA Factory, Axolotl, and Unsloth all assume a pretrained checkpoint as the starting point. Oumi supports training from scratch but targets standard architectures. None of these tools provide a systematic framework for experimenting with novel sequence mixer architectures, comparing diverse optimization algorithms under controlled conditions, or exploring the interaction between architectural choices and training dynamics.

Frankenstein Transformer fills this gap by providing a schema-first configuration system purpose-built for architecture experimentation. Its key differentiators include:

  • 43 sequence mixers spanning dense attention, recurrent/retentive blocks, sparse attention patterns, gated mechanisms, adaptive depth routing, and conditional memory layers, all selectable via a single YAML field.

  • 23 optimizer families with a prefixed hyperparameter routing system that enables per-parameter-group control across embeddings, normalization layers, attention blocks, and feed-forward networks.

  • Dual training modes supporting both encoder-style masked language modeling (MLM) and decoder-style autoregressive (AR) next-token prediction, with specialized fine-tuning workflows for each.

  • Strict schema validation via additionalProperties: false constraints that prevent configuration errors before training begins, ensuring reproducibility across experiments.

  • End-to-end workflows spanning quantized deployment (ternary weight packing, INT8 activations) and sentence-embedding training inspired by SBERT .

  • Web-based configuration interface providing schema-driven form rendering with inline documentation, real-time validation, and CLI command generation.

By decoupling architecture definition from training infrastructure through a validated configuration contract, Frankenstein Transformer enables systematic comparison of sequence mixer families and optimization strategies under identical training conditions—a capability not provided by any existing tool in the ecosystem.

System Design and Architecture

Configuration-Centric Architecture

Experimentation in this project is schema first. Rather than exposing loosely checked flags, model topology, optimizer family, training limits, and telemetry pass through a single validated configuration document, which reduces ambiguity when reproducing results and lets many architectures share one operational interface.

The authoritative contract is , a modular JSON Schema whose modules under cover the model, model class, tokenizer, optimizer, SBERT, training, and dataset blocks. The top-level objects are base_model, tokenizer, model_class, model, training, image, vision_dataset, and text_dataset.

Model class.

The model_class field selects among three variants:

  • frankenstein_text_encoder: mixed-architecture encoder with the full range of sequence mixers, MoE, and advanced normalization, trained with masked language modeling.

  • frankenstein_text_decoder: autoregressive causal decoder for next-token generation; the runtime forces decoder masking.

  • frankenstein_vit: Vision Transformer over image patches for masked patch prediction, classification, and segmentation; the runtime forces encoder masking and the configuration requires the image and vision_dataset blocks.

Training mode.

model.dims.mode controls masking: encoder uses bidirectional attention for masked language modeling, and decoder uses causal masking for autoregressive prediction.

Mixer selection.

model.dims.layer_pattern is an ordered list of mixer identifiers drawn from the eight families described in Section 4; the schema fixes the accepted identifiers, and the complete enumeration appears in Figure 2 and Appendix 14.

Optimizer selection.

training.optimizer.optimizer_class selects one of twenty-four optimizer families, summarized in Section 5 and detailed in Appendix 15.

Schema Scope and Validation Rules

Top-level and nested objects set additionalProperties: false, so unknown keys fail fast instead of being silently ignored. Optimizer parameters are further constrained by per-family prefix rules. Cross-component validation rejects incompatible combinations before training: hidden size must be divisible by the number of heads, the number of key–value heads must divide the number of heads, vocabulary size must match the tokenizer, a base model requires a task and (for MLM) a tokenizer, each task requires its matching optimizer block, BitNet router flags require BitNet to be enabled, and the decoder and vision classes force their respective masking modes.

Configuration Schema

The complete schema—fields, types, ranges, and validation rules—is documented in Appendix 13. Looped blocks are configured through num_layers and num_loops, giving num_layers\(\times\)num_loops logical layers at fixed parameter count.

Training Tasks

training.task selects the objective: mlm (masked language modeling), causal_lm (autoregressive next-token prediction, decoder class only), sbert (sentence embeddings), text_classification (encoder class only), and the vision tasks patch_prediction, classification, and segmentation (Vision Transformer only). NLP tasks consume text_dataset; vision tasks consume vision_dataset. Sentence-embedding workflows are described in Section 7.

Training Safety and Runtime Semantics

The training step accumulates gradients over micro-batches, clips the global norm, checks for post-clip overflow, retries a bounded number of times on non-finite values, dispatches the configured scheduler, and rotates rolling and best checkpoints. When training.test_percentage is positive, a deterministic fraction of the dataset is held out before training and the final weights are evaluated on it; the loss and task accuracy (character error rate for ASR) are written to test_metrics.json. A single training.seed (default \(42\)) controls the run’s randomness: it seeds the Python, NumPy, PyTorch and CUDA generators, model weight initialization, DataLoader shuffle generators and workers, and the held-out permutation, and it enables deterministic cuDNN, so repeated runs on the same hardware and software stack reproduce initialization, batch order and split. The full pseudocode and the split formulation are deferred to Appendix 20.

Normalization Variants

Normalization is both a modeling choice and a schema compatibility question. The accepted norm.type values are layer_norm, dynamic_tanh, derf, rms_norm, prms_norm (partial RMSNorm), and flash_norm (weightless RMSNorm). Their formulations and comparison are detailed in Appendix 20.

Residual-Stream Architectures

Residual connections are exposed as a macro-design choice through the model.residuals block:

  • Standard: the classical identity residual .

  • None: no skip connection, retained only as an ablation probe.

  • Attention Residuals (full_attn or block_attn): learned attention over depth replaces the fixed residual sum, either over all previous layers or over block-wise summaries .

  • Manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mhc.enabled): an \(n\)-stream residual whose mixing matrix is constrained to the Birkhoff polytope .

Attention Residuals compose with mHC and Mixture-of-Depths; the formulations, wiring, and reported results are collected in Appendices 23 and 22.

Architecture Taxonomy and Implementation

Attention and Sequence-Mixer Families

The system implements forty-seven sequence mixers organized into ten functional categories that reflect how each method balances expressivity, computational cost, and memory.

  1. Dense baselines (3): standard softmax attention, sigmoid attention, and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) provide full global routing at quadratic cost.

  2. Recurrent and retentive (4): RetNet, Mamba, ODE-style blocks, and Titans maintain state for constant-time inference through recurrence, selective state spaces, continuous depth, or test-time memory.

  3. Sparse patterns (12): Sparse Transformer, Longformer, SWA with attention sinks, BigBird, SparseK, NSA, SpargeAttn, FASA, MSA, SparDA, LSA, and Fast Conformer reduce quadratic cost through structured sparsity, token selection, training-free pruning, or semantic key clustering.

  4. Gated mechanisms (8): GLA, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet-2, HGRN2, FoX, Gated Softmax, and KDA introduce data-dependent control over retention, forgetting, and update strength.

  5. Latent compression (10): MLA, GQLA, MLRA, Tucker, IHA, GTA, MTLA, CCA, CCGQA, and GMA compress key–value state into low-rank bottlenecks or route through a Gaussian-mixture latent memory.

  6. Conditional memory (1): Engram provides test-time read/write memory through learned lookups.

  7. Token-indexed memory (1): Memory Attention replaces the dedicated value projection with layer-specific token memory, constructing values as \(V = K + \mathrm{Norm}(E[s])\) while keeping the softmax weighting unchanged .

  8. Fast-weight attention (6): Falcon-1/2/3 and Falcon-1A/2A/3A treat the recurrent state transition as an online continual-learning rule .

  9. Geometric field (1): SSOG applies a structured geometric prior over the attention matrix .

  10. Convolution-augmented (1): the Conformer block fuses multi-head self-attention with a depthwise-convolution module between two Macaron feed-forward layers, giving every layer a local branch alongside the global receptive field (Appendix 30).

Dense and Recurrent Families

The dense baselines—standard softmax and sigmoid attention —and the recurrent family—RetNet , Mamba , ODE-style blocks , and Titans —define the expressiveness-versus-efficiency trade-off. Formulations, parallel and recurrent forms, pseudocode, and a comparison table are collected in Appendix 16.

Token-Indexed Memory Family

Memory Attention keeps the standard softmax attention operator but removes the dedicated value projection: values are the contextual keys plus a layer-specific, token-ID-indexed memory row, \(V = K + \mathrm{Norm}(E[s])\), with RoPE applied only to the scoring pair. This increases parameter capacity without proportional dense computation and retains a conventional KV cache at inference.

Latent and Low-Rank Attention Family

This family compresses per-token key–value state into a low-rank latent: MLA, GQLA, MLRA, Tucker, IHA, GTA, and MTLA unify grouped-query, latent, factorized, and temporal designs. CCA and CCGQA formulate attention in a compressed latent with decoupled grouping, while GMA replaces pairwise interaction with probabilistic routing through learned Gaussian-mixture components. Formulations, pseudocode, and a comparison table are collected in Appendix 17.

Sparse Attention Extensions

The registry includes twelve sparse blocks . Two inference-time methods, fasa and sparge, apply their sparse heuristic only when the model is in evaluation mode: during training the enclosing hybrid layer substitutes standard dense attention over the same \(\mathbf{q}/\mathbf{k}/\mathbf{v}/\mathbf{o}\) projections, so the trained weights are exactly the ones the sparse path reads at inference. swa is also training-free but is a normal trainable mixer, so it runs its windowed pattern in both training and inference. LSA is the family’s semantic selector: keys are pooled and Ward-clustered per 512-token block, and each query scores the cached bucket centroids instead of every key, selecting top-\(p\) buckets that expand into its \(k\) long-range keys on top of sinks and a one-block window. Fast Conformer is the family’s long-form broadcast pattern: a fixed local window plus a global attention token pinned at the sequence head, optionally with its own query/key/value projections, giving bounded-memory decoding at hours-long context. Formulations, pseudocode, per-block characteristics, and a comparison table are collected in Appendix 18.

Gated and Fast-Weight Attention

The gated family contains eight blocks . Gating controls what information survives, either in recurrent state updates (GLA, DeltaNet variants, HGRN2, KDA) or in the full attention path (FoX, Gated Softmax). Formulations, pseudocode, and a comparison table are collected in Appendix 19.

Fast-weight attention recasts the recurrent update as an online continual-learning rule; the six Falcon variants unify DeltaNet-style regression and linear-attention writes under read-after-write semantics with normalized step sizes and explicit forgetting. Each variant ships a recurrent reference scan and a chunk-parallel kernel. Formulations, configuration knobs, and published results are collected in Appendix 27.

Optimizer Families and Training Dynamics

Optimizing large transformer architectures is complicated by non-convex landscapes, saddle points, and heterogeneous parameter groups. The system supports thirty-six optimizer families in eight categories: classical baselines (SGD with momentum, AdamW, RAdam); momentum and variance reduction (Adan, ADOPT, AdEMAMix, MARS, Cautious AdamW); memory-efficient and low-rank methods (Adafactor, GaLore, Lion, APOLLO, APOLLO-Mini, Q-APOLLO, AdamPM); schedule-free and parameter-free methods (Schedule-Free AdamW, Prodigy) with large-batch scaling (LAMB); curvature-aware and second-order methods (Sophia, Shampoo, SOAP); geometry-oriented methods (Muon, Turbo-Muon, AF-Muon, AdaMuon, Dion3, ROOT, Muon², NorMuon, Conda, TUON, NAMO, NAMO-D); adaptivity-tunable optimizers (Anon); and evolutionary population-based hybrids (EvE, EA4LLM). Algorithms, pseudocode, and memory and complexity comparisons are collected in Appendix 15.

Quantization and Deployment

The deploy stage converts a trained checkpoint into a compact artifact through ternary weight packing and INT8 activation scaling, with size estimates aligned with lightweight deployment goals . The same subcommand emits standard or quantized artifacts, or exports HuggingFace Transformers and BitNet GGUF formats for external runtimes. The formulations and size estimates are deferred to Appendix 20.

SBERT Downstream Tasks

Sentence embedding is built on Siamese-style training . For sentence pair \((s_1,s_2)\) with embeddings \((e_1,e_2)\): \[\text{cos}(e_1,e_2)=\frac{e_1^\top e_2}{\|e_1\|\|e_2\|}\] and regression-style cosine loss: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{cos}}=\left(\text{cos}(e_1,e_2)-y\right)^2\] with \(y\in[-1,1]\) in this pipeline.

Supported downstream modes:

  • Similarity: pairwise score between two sentences.

  • Search: top-\(k\) nearest neighbors over a corpus.

  • Cluster: grouping embeddings (e.g., k-means).

  • Encode: persistent embedding export for later retrieval.

The pseudocode for the SBERT inference mode router—dispatching among similarity, search, cluster, and encode modes over a shared encoder—is deferred to Appendix 20.

No-Code Integration: The dashai-frankenstein Plugin

The CLI and web builder described in Section 3 serve researchers comfortable with YAML configuration files. A complementary audience—domain specialists, educators, and analysts who need a trained model but not a training script—is better served by a graphical environment. Frankenstein Transformer therefore ships dashai-frankenstein, an adapter that registers its model classes as components of dashAI (https://github.com/DashAISoftware/dashAI), an open-source, local-first machine-learning workbench developed by a Chilean academic consortium (Universidad de Chile/FCFM, CENIA, IMFD, and ANID funding). Both systems are schema-driven—dashAI renders forms from Pydantic schemas, Frankenstein validates YAML against a strict JSON Schema—so the integration leaves dashAI’s backend untouched; the plugin is discovered through the standard dashai.plugins entry-points group documented in dashAI’s plugin guide (https://docs.dash-ai.com/learn/guides/plugins/).

Registered Components

A single entry-points group registers five components:

  • FrankensteinMLMModel (BaseModel, TextClassificationTask): encoder with a classification head over pooled output; predict returns per-class probabilities.

  • FrankensteinDecoderModel (BaseGenerativeModel, TextToTextGenerationTask): forces the decoder class and exposes autoregressive top-\(k\) sampling.

  • FrankensteinViTClassifier (BaseModel, ImageClassificationTask): uses the ViT classification head (Appendix 24).

  • FrankensteinViTSegmenter (BaseModel, plugin SegmentationTask): uses the ViT segmentation head and returns per-pixel class maps.

  • SegmentationTask (BaseTask): declares the image-in/mask-out contract that dashAI does not ship.

All share one thin facade over the engine API, so the plugin has a single heavy dependency.

Passthrough Configuration Schema

The Frankenstein JSON Schema remains the single source of truth instead of translating its fields into native dashAI forms. Each component exposes one frankenstein_json field holding a complete training configuration as single-line JSON. Before any training runs, the adapter parses the JSON, validates it against the resolved schema, and applies the config loader’s cross-component checks; failures surface as a readable error tagged with the failing stage. Dataset adapters map dashAI datasets onto Frankenstein’s expectations, inject the vocabulary size from the resolved tokenizer, and stream per-epoch metrics back to dashAI.

Status

The three implementation phases—classification MVP, generative decoder and ViT classifier, and ViT segmenter—are complete, but the package has not yet run inside a live dashAI instance and PyPI publication is pending. Known limitations include a direct classification loop rather than MLM pretraining, deferred native form fields for high-leverage knobs, and unconfirmed rendering of segmentation masks. The adapter deliberately leaves dashAI’s core untouched, so future releases cannot break it through coupling.

Empirical Evaluation

The preceding sections describe the toolkit in terms of what it can express: which mixers, optimizers, normalizations, and deployment paths the schema admits. This section turns from design to evidence and reports what happened when that design was exercised at scale. Every mixer pair, every optimizer, and every deployment path in the study was trained, exported, quantized, and evaluated through the same YAML interface, so the measurements that follow are comparable by construction: a difference between two configurations reflects the configurations themselves, not differences in the plumbing around them.

The campaign is organised in rounds. A round is one complete pass of the experiment harness over a generated set of configurations, from training through reporting. Round 1 was a rehearsal at smoke scale—5,129 stage records, with training runs of roughly half a minute each—whose purpose was to debug the pipeline itself before committing serious computation. Round 2 is the measurement campaign analysed here: 868 configurations trained end-to-end, 2,656,372 logged optimisation steps, and 905 CPU-hours of training across those runs, published as an interactive report with downloadable datasets so that every number below can be rederived without re-running anything.1

Two appendices accompany this section and serve complementary purposes. Appendix 33 documents the harness—the five-stage pipeline, the three independent recorders, the consolidated datasets, and the reporting toolchain—in enough detail that launching a new round reduces to pointing the same scripts at a new folder. Appendix 34 reports Round 2 in full, with the parameter census, the training curves, the complete A\(\times\)B atlas of mixer pairs, the ablation sweeps, and the deployment measurements. The present section states the findings and interprets them; the appendices carry the supporting evidence.

What One Round Measures

Every configuration passes through the same five stages, shown in Figure 12: it is trained for 100 epochs, its checkpoint is exported, the checkpoint is deployed twice (once in a standard format, once in a post-training-quantized format), the two deployed models are evaluated on four held-out masked prompts each, and a Hugging Face package is exported. A single YAML file drives all five stages: it selects the model (one mixer, a pair of mixers declared as layer_pattern: [A, B], a vision transformer, or an ablation of the backbone), the task, and the training budget. Because the file is the only input, any measurement can be traced back to the configuration that produced it, and any configuration can be re-run to reproduce its measurement.

Three recorders observe the process independently and are joined only at reporting time: a per-step training log, a parameter census by module group, and a ledger with one row per stage execution. Independence is a deliberate safeguard—no single recorder can silently corrupt the picture, and a disagreement between recorders is itself a diagnostic. The report joins all three by configuration slug, a short identifier derived mechanically from the YAML file.

Round 2 was generated programmatically rather than curated by hand. The hybrid pairs are all combinations of the 42-entry mixer list taken two at a time, materialised as a two-layer model whose layer 0 runs mixer A and layer 1 runs mixer B; single-mixer baselines use one layer. Because the combinations follow the fixed order of the list, no reversed pair \((B, A)\) exists: the campaign measures A__B but never B__A. The “first versus second mixer” asymmetry reported below is therefore confounded with list order—position in the stack coincides with position in the list—and must be read descriptively rather than causally. The families differ in what they hold fixed, and the distinction guides every comparison that follows. The hybrid pairs and singles vary the mixer stack itself. The optimizer, structural, normalization, and positional-encoding families share the same 210k-parameter backbone and vary exactly one component—which is precisely what makes them ablations. The task, tokenizer, batch-size, real-data, and audio families change the objective or the data, and therefore the loss scale, which is why they are never compared directly against the mixer sweep.

Findings

Six findings summarise the round. Each is stated as a claim, supported by a measurement, and followed by its interpretation.

The second mixer is the stronger lever. For each candidate mixer \(B\), consider the mean final loss over all pairs in which \(B\) occupies the second position. This marginal mean ranges from 9.37 nats (sparsek) to 10.18 (mamba)—a spread of 0.81 nats. The corresponding range for the first position is only 0.55 nats (9.26–9.81, restricted to mixers with enough pairs for a stable mean). The same asymmetry appears when the atlas is read geometrically: column by column (fixed B, varying A), a good second mixer keeps almost every first mixer inside the 8.9–9.6 nat band, while row by row (fixed A, varying B), no first mixer rescues a bad second one. In other words, the pair inherits its ceiling from its second layer, and at this scale the choice of B is worth roughly 1.5\(\times\) the choice of A. Losses are reported in nats—the natural-logarithm unit of cross-entropy—so a gap of 0.81 nats corresponds to a factor of \(e^{0.81} \approx 2.2\times\) in the geometric-mean likelihood assigned to the correct token.

Pairing is not additive. If mixers contributed independently, the loss of a pair would be predictable from its parts. It is not. Define the marginal mean \(\mu_M\) as the mean loss of all pairs containing mixer \(M\), and the synergy of a pair as the average of its two marginals minus its measured loss, \(S_{A,B} = (\mu_A + \mu_B)/2 - L_{A,B}\): positive synergy means the pair is better than its parts suggest, negative means worse. The best interaction is nsa+engram at \(+1.304\) nats and the worst is gqa+tucker at \(-1.018\). The positive tail consistently pairs a cheap, stable first mixer with a memory-heavy second one; the negative tail is dominated by second mixers that look average in isolation (gta, gqa, tucker) but clash when stacked after a strong first mixer. The practical consequence is that the atlas cannot be summarised by two ranked lists: interaction noise of \(\pm 0.3\) nats is larger than the difference between most optimizers in the ablation.

Scale is a weak lever at this size. Within the hybrid pairs, the parameter count correlates with final loss at \(r = -0.20\) and with held-out accuracy at \(r = -0.07\): at this scale, adding parameters barely buys quality. What parameters do predict reliably is cost (\(r = 0.68\) with step time, \(r = 0.65\) with wall-clock). The largest model of the round (engram__conformer, 415,904 parameters) is not the best. Across all 868 rows the correlation appears much stronger (\(r = -0.43\) for loss), but this is a family confound in the manner of Simpson’s paradox: vision transformers are simultaneously larger and far easier to fit than MLM pairs, so the pooled coefficient measures the gap between families rather than the effect of size. The comparison of interest is the within-pairs one, and there size is close to irrelevant.

Post-training quantization is essentially free. Quantization here means converting trained weights to a lower-precision format after training, with no retraining. Of the 810 configurations deployed in both formats, 800 keep an identical top-5 hit rate; the mean top-1 moves from 5.62% to 5.43% and the mean top-5 from 13.36% to 13.24%—deltas of \(-0.19\) and \(-0.12\) percentage points, within the resolution of a four-sentence evaluation. Quantized deployment is not faster end-to-end—it wins in only 32.3% of runs, with a median ratio of 0.64\(\times\)—because the deployment stage is dominated by serialisation and format conversion rather than by arithmetic. Evaluation itself, which does measure inference, is faster in 51.2% of runs with a median 1.03\(\times\) speed-up. The quality claim is firm (quantization does not move the metrics); the speed claim is about the pipeline, not the format.

The sweep is honest about its failures and its blind spots. The ledger holds 5,271 stage records, of which 275 are failures (171 in training, 104 in deployment); all of them fall outside the 868 analysed configurations, which were selected precisely because they trained. Four mixers (cca, ccgqa, msa, ssog) never train in any configuration, which accounts exactly for the 158 missing cells of the 861-cell atlas. Four others (standard, bigbird, longformer, titan) produce bit-identical losses because their attention windows (at least 64 tokens) cover the whole 32-token sequence—at this context length they collapse to the same dense model, and the atlas measures one model four times. Separately, the ledger records 37 pairs under both retnet and the now-removed retnet_attn alias with identical metrics—one implementation under two names—which the analysis collapses. Reporting these defects explicitly is a design choice: a silent zero or a hidden duplicate would contaminate every downstream statistic.

The vision block works. Segmentation reaches 90.7% mean held-out accuracy, classification 75.8%, and patch prediction 69.9%—an order of magnitude above the MLM pairs. The gap reflects the difficulty of the tasks, not the quality of the mixers: guessing a masked token in a 512-token vocabulary is harder than the vision objectives at this scale. This is why the families are kept separate throughout the report, and why no cross-family ranking is stated.

Threats to Validity

The findings above are conditioned on the scale of the round, and four limitations should temper their reading.

  • Scale and convergence. The models are small (127k–416k parameters), the vocabulary is 512 Spanish tokens, the sequences are 32 tokens long, and each configuration trains for 100 epochs with a single seed. Every learning curve is still descending at epoch 100, so the ranking rewards fast learners rather than converged quality.

  • Resolution of the evaluation signal. Inference uses four sentences per configuration. One additional correct token moves a top-5 rate by 25 percentage points, so the held-out signal is a smoke detector for catastrophic failures, not a ranking instrument.

  • Optimizer ties. Several optimizers converge to the same loss because the run is too short to separate them; the optimizer ranking is indicative at best.

  • Known failure modes. One text-classification run collapsed to a constant prediction—a failure mode recorded as such, not a usable model—and the four never-training mixers and the retnet alias are carried forward as explicit caveats.

The rankings in Appendix 34 are therefore directional: they indicate where to look next, not final verdicts. The next round should re-run the atlas at 256–512 tokens, with a 200-sentence evaluation set, at least three seeds, and 300 epochs for the top pairs.

Discussion

The design choices in Frankenstein Transformer reflect several engineering and research tensions in modern deep learning tooling.

The campaign reported in Section 9 turns several of those tensions into measurements rather than opinions. The strict schema paid off operationally: 868 configurations trained, deployed and were evaluated through the same contract, and the failures that remained were concentrated in four mixers and in checkpoint serialisation, not in configuration drift. The prefixed optimizer system proved expressive but, at 100 epochs, undecisive—a dozen optimizers converged to the same loss—which is itself an argument for the schema: only a controlled sweep can show that a design dimension does not matter at a given scale.

Schema-Driven Design Trade-offs

The schema-first approach provides significant reproducibility benefits by enforcing explicit contracts and failing fast on invalid configurations. However, this approach also introduces rigidity: adding new architectures or optimizers requires schema extensions rather than loose command-line arguments. The prefixed hyperparameter system enables fine-grained control but increases configuration complexity for users accustomed to simpler interfaces.

The decision to enforce additionalProperties: false at all schema levels eliminates silent parameter swallowing that has plagued earlier configuration systems, but this strictness requires careful schema maintenance when extending system capabilities. Each new attention mechanism or optimizer variant must be properly integrated into the validation framework, including schema field definitions with appropriate types and constraints, prefixed hyperparameter mapping for optimizer-specific groups, default values aligned with research best practices, and documentation strings for web interface rendering.

Architectural Coverage and Gaps

The forty-seven implemented mixers span the major research directions in sequence modeling, but certain gaps remain. The system lacks recent hybrid architectures such as Griffin and Jamba , which combine gating with state-space models. MoE routing is implemented for FFN layers but not for attention computation, where recent work has shown benefits .

The sparse attention coverage is broad. The two inference-time methods (FASA, SpargeAttn) keep their training-free character in the sense that their sparsification rule is never learned; instead, the implementation trains the layer as standard dense attention over the same projections and activates the sparse selection/pruning path only at evaluation, so both mixers can be trained from scratch and their sparse behaviour is exactly the one described in the original papers.

The gated and fast-weight coverage spans the major categories, including the six Falcon variants . Residual-stream macro-design is covered by Attention Residuals and by the manifold-constrained \(n\)-stream residual (mHC) , whose Sinkhorn–Knopp projection onto the Birkhoff polytope restores the identity-mapping property lost by unconstrained hyper-connections; mHC is validated only at the level of the published 3B–27B MoE experiments and would benefit from independent reproductions at smaller scales (Appendix 22).

Optimizer Landscape Fragmentation

The support for twenty-four optimizer families across seven categories demonstrates comprehensiveness but also highlights the fragmented state of optimization research. Users face significant decision complexity when choosing among variance-reduction methods (Adan, MARS), memory-efficient variants (GaLore, Adafactor, APOLLO), and curvature-aware approaches (Sophia, Shampoo). The prefixed hyperparameter system, while powerful, requires understanding of which parameters are relevant for each optimizer class.

The implementation quality varies across optimizers: classical methods (AdamW, SGD with momentum) are highly optimized in PyTorch, while newer methods (Muon, Turbo-Muon, AF-Muon, SOAP) may require custom implementations that affect numerical stability and performance characteristics.

Deployment and Production Considerations

The quantization pipeline demonstrates practical deployment concerns but makes specific engineering trade-offs. Ternary weight packing reduces storage to approximately \(1.58\) bits per parameter, but this aggressive compression may degrade performance, especially for smaller models where quantization error is more significant. The current implementation applies quantization uniformly across parameter types.

The SBERT workflows provide practical utility for semantic similarity and retrieval tasks, but implementation assumes standard pooling strategies (CLS token, mean pooling). Recent advances such as Matryoshka embeddings and contrastive learning refinements are not yet incorporated.

Integration and Extensibility Challenges

The current codebase structure, while functional, presents maintenance challenges as architecture and optimizer families expand. The dispatcher pattern for mixer selection and optimizer routing handles extensibility but risks becoming a “kitchen sink” of conditional logic. Future versions would benefit from plugin-based architectures where new mixers and optimizers could be registered declaratively rather than modifying core dispatch logic.

The web configuration interface provides significant usability improvements but introduces deployment complexity: running Streamlit alongside training jobs requires additional resources and infrastructure considerations that may not be appropriate for all environments, particularly HPC clusters without web access.

Conclusion

Frankenstein Transformer presents a unified, configuration-driven experimentation platform addressing three challenges in modern deep learning research: architectural fragmentation across dense attention, recurrent models, sparse patterns, gated mechanisms, latent compression, conditional memory, fast-weight memories, and geometric priors; optimizer landscape complexity spanning classical baselines, variance-reduction methods, memory-efficient variants, schedule-free approaches, curvature-aware algorithms, and geometry-oriented methods; and end-to-end deployment workflows spanning quantization and sentence embedding.

The system’s primary contributions are:

  1. Schema-First Design: A strict YAML-based configuration contract with validation and prefixed hyperparameter routing enabling reproducible experiments across forty-seven sequence mixers and twenty-four optimizer families.

  2. Comprehensive Architecture Support: Implementation spanning dense baselines, recurrent and retentive blocks, sparse attention, gated mechanisms, latent compression, conditional memory, fast-weight attention, and geometric-field attention, with encoder, decoder, and Vision Transformer model classes.

  3. Unified Optimizer Framework: Prefixed hyperparameter groups enabling fine-grained control over embeddings, normalization layers, attention weights, and the remaining parameters across classical baselines (SGD+Momentum, AdamW, RAdam), variance reduction (Adan, ADOPT, AdEMAMix, MARS, Cautious), memory-efficient and low-rank methods (Adafactor, GaLore, Lion, APOLLO, APOLLO-Mini, Q-APOLLO), large-batch and schedule simplification (LAMB, Schedule-Free AdamW, Prodigy), curvature-aware (Sophia), second-order (Shampoo, SOAP), geometry-oriented (Muon, Turbo-Muon, AF-Muon), and adaptivity-tunable (Anon) optimizers.

  4. End-to-End Workflows: Integrated deployment pipeline supporting ternary weight packing and INT8 activation quantization; SBERT-inspired training and inference for semantic similarity, retrieval, and clustering tasks.

  5. Interactive Configuration: Streamlit-based web interface providing schema-driven form generation, real-time validation, inline documentation, and CLI command synthesis.

This system enables rapid experimental iteration while maintaining reproducibility through strict configuration contracts. By consolidating diverse research contributions into a unified toolkit, it lowers barriers to exploring novel architectures and optimization strategies, particularly for researchers who may lack resources to implement and validate each variant independently.

Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations and promising directions for future work emerge from this system’s design and implementation:

  1. Architecture Integration: Recent hybrid architectures (Griffin, Jamba, Mamba-X) demonstrate benefits of combining multiple mechanisms into unified blocks. Future versions should integrate these architectures and explore systematic composition patterns.

  2. Advanced Quantization: Current implementation uses uniform ternary packing across all parameters. Research on layer-wise, channel-wise, and importance-aware quantization suggests more sophisticated strategies could improve quality-efficiency trade-offs.

  3. Plugin-Based Extensibility: The current dispatch pattern becomes increasingly complex with each new addition. A plugin architecture allowing declarative registration of new mixers, optimizers, and normalization methods would improve maintainability and reduce risk of bugs in core dispatch logic.

  4. Automated Hyperparameter Optimization: The schema supports extensive hyperparameter spaces, but users must manually explore these spaces. Integration with Bayesian optimization, multi-armed bandit strategies, or gradient-based hyperparameter tuning could automate effective configuration discovery.

  5. Production Deployment: The web interface improves usability but may not be appropriate for all deployment environments. Headless configuration modes, API-based configuration management, or improved CLI ergonomics could serve HPC and production workflows.

  6. Evaluation Benchmarking: Round 2 (Section 9) provides the first comparative atlas across the mixer list, but it is a 32-token, single-seed, 100-epoch measurement. Future rounds should extend it to longer context, more held-out sentences and multiple seeds before the rankings are read as architectural conclusions.

  7. Training Stability Guarantees: Current implementation includes NaN/Inf guards and gradient clipping, but formal analysis of stability conditions for different mixer-optimizer combinations, particularly with looped blocks and aggressive quantization, remains open.

  8. Multimodal and Task-Specific Extensions: The current design covers text and single-image tasks through the Vision Transformer class. Extensions to vision-language models, multimodal architectures, and task-specific fine-tuning workflows (e.g., instruction tuning, RLHF) would broaden applicability.

The research trajectory of sequence modeling continues toward hybrid approaches that combine the strengths of multiple paradigms—compression from recurrence, selectivity from attention, gating for memory management, and sparsity for efficiency. A unified experimentation platform like Frankenstein Transformer becomes increasingly valuable as this convergence accelerates, enabling researchers to explore this expanding design space with reproducible, well-engineered infrastructure.

Conceptual Introduction—Transformers and Attention for Beginners

This appendix provides an accessible introduction to the fundamental concepts of transformers and the attention mechanism, aimed at readers without deep prior knowledge in deep learning. Transformers are the engine behind modern artificial intelligence systems like ChatGPT, but their operation can be understood through real-world analogies.

What is a Transformer?

A transformer is a neural architecture that processes text or data sequences by interpreting the meaning of each word while considering all other words in context. Imagine you read a sentence:

“The bank was full of people waiting. Mary went to the bank.”

What does “bank” mean in each case? In the first sentence, it refers to a financial institution (or a bench). In the second, it is less clear without context. A transformer solves this automatically by looking at all surrounding words. In the second sentence, seeing “Mary went”, the model better understands that it probably is a riverbank (where she goes to swim) or a financial institution (where she goes to conduct a transaction).

This ability to understand the complete meaning of a word by considering the entire sentence is called contextualization, and it is the heart of how modern transformers work.

The Attention Mechanism: An Analogy

The attention mechanism is the “magic trick” that allows transformers to understand context. Think of it as participating in an important conversation in a noisy room:

  1. Lots of noise: Someone is speaking and being very important to you.

  2. You ignore the rest: Your brain automatically focuses attention on that person, ignoring other sounds.

  3. You understand better: By concentrating, you catch every word clearly.

The neural attention mechanism works the same way: each word “asks” how important every other word is to understanding its meaning, then “focuses” its attention on the most relevant ones.

Practical Example Step-by-Step

Let’s see how a transformer understands the word “eats” in two different contexts:

Context 1: “The cat eats fish”

The transformer, when processing “eats”, internally asks:

  • How relevant is “The”? Little (it’s just an article). Low attention.

  • How relevant is “cat”? Very relevant (it’s the subject, who eats). High attention.

  • How relevant is “fish”? Very relevant (it’s what is eaten). High attention.

Thus, the mental representation of “eats” focuses primarily on “cat” and “fish”.

Context 2: “The restaurant eats into profit margins”

Here the transformer asks in a different context:

  • How relevant is “restaurant”? Very relevant (it’s the subject). High attention.

  • How relevant is “profit”? Very relevant (it’s affected). High attention.

  • How relevant is “margins”? Very relevant (it’s what’s being consumed). High attention.

The word “eats” gets a completely different representation because it “attends” to different words in different contexts.

How Attention Works Mathematically (Simple Version)

Behind the attention shift is mathematics. Here is the simplified version without too much technical detail:

Step 1: Queries, Keys, and Values

Each word in the sentence is transformed into three versions:

  • Query: “What information do I need to know?”

  • Key: “What information do I have?”

  • Value: “Here is my important information.”

Imagine in a library, each visitor is a “query”, each book is a “key”, and the content is the “value”. The librarian (attention) matches queries with the most relevant keys to access the correct value.

Step 2: Compatibility

The system examines how compatible each query is with each key. Queries similar to keys get a high compatibility score. This is calculated by multiplying the query by the key (mathematically, the dot product).

Step 3: Focus

The compatibility scores are converted into “focus weights”. High compatibilities mean “focus attention here”, and low ones mean “ignore this”. Mathematically, a function called softmax converts scores into percentages (like: 40% attention here, 35% here, 25% there).

Step 4: Combine

Finally, the system combines all values, weighted by the focus weights. If a word has 80% attention on the subject, 80% of the subject’s information gets blended into that word’s representation.

Multiple Attention Heads: Multiple Perspectives

A key feature is that transformers do not use a single attention but multiple attention heads in parallel. It’s as if you had 8 people analyzing the sentence simultaneously, each paying attention to different aspects:

  • Person 1: “I focus on subject-verb relationships.”

  • Person 2: “I search for the direct object.”

  • Person 3: “I track information about verb tense.”

  • Person 4: “I search for modifiers and adjectives.”

Each “head” learns to focus on different language patterns. Together, they capture much richer understanding than a single head.

Stacking Layers

Transformers process information in multiple layers (usually 12 to 48 for practical models). Imagine editing an essay:

  1. First pass: You fix spelling and basic grammar.

  2. Second pass: You improve clarity and sentence structure.

  3. Third pass: You ensure consistency and narrative flow.

Transformers work the same way: each layer refines text understanding. The first layer captures basic features (simple words, genders), while later layers understand complex concepts (word relationships, abstract meanings).

Why Does It Matter?

The attention mechanism was revolutionary because:

  1. Parallelism: It finds context for any word with any other word, without processing them sequentially (unlike earlier systems). This makes it very fast.

  2. Flexibility: It learns what patterns to look for automatically from data, without you needing to program rules manually.

  3. Scalability: It works from small texts to contexts with millions of words.

  4. General Capabilities: The same mechanism works for translation, summarization, question-answering, text generation, computer vision, and more.

Practical Challenges

Despite the extraordinary success of transformers, they present challenges:

Computational Complexity

If a sentence has 1,000 words, the standard attention mechanism must compare each word with all other 1,000 words. That’s \(1,000 \times 1,000 = 1,000,000\) comparisons. For long documents with millions of words, this becomes prohibitively expensive in time and memory.

Memory Requirements

Especially during inference (when using trained models), storing the entire attention matrix can consume enormous amounts of RAM or GPU memory, limiting the sequence lengths you can process.

Device Efficiency

Transformers were designed for powerful TPUs and GPUs. Running them on phones or embedded devices is challenging.

Modern Solutions

To solve these challenges, research has proposed many variants:

  • Sparse Attention: Instead of comparing each word with ALL others, it compares only with a strategic subset (nearby neighbors, periodic patterns). Reduces complexity from \(\mathcal{O}(n^2)\) to \(\mathcal{O}(n \log n)\) or \(\mathcal{O}(n)\).

  • Recurrent Models: Like Mamba, they incorporate aspects of old recurrent neural networks but with better modern efficiency.

  • Gated Attention: Mechanisms that selectively learn what information to pass forward, reducing storage needs.

  • Quantization: Use smaller numbers (integers instead of decimals) to reduce memory without losing too much precision.

These innovations are what this toolkit (Frankenstein) allows you to experiment with easily.

Key Takeaways

  • A transformer is a neural network that understands language context very well.

  • The attention mechanism allows each word to “focus” on which other words are relevant to understanding its meaning.

  • Attention works by computing compatibility between each word (query) and all others (keys), then combining information based on that compatibility (values).

  • Multiple heads of attention explore different patterns in parallel.

  • Multiple layers progressively refine understanding.

  • The main challenge is that standard attention has quadratic complexity, which is expensive for long texts.

  • Many modern solutions (sparse attention, recurrent models, quantization) address these challenges, and this toolkit lets you explore all of them.

Configuration Schema Structure

The Frankenstein Transformer toolkit enforces a strict YAML configuration schema with additionalProperties: false at all levels. The schema is defined in , which references modular sub-schemas in . Every configurable field must be declared in the schema; unrecognized keys are rejected at validation time. This appendix documents the complete schema structure, including all fields, their types, constraints, and cross-component validation rules.

Top-Level Structure

The root schema object has the following top-level properties. All are optional except training, which is required:

  • base_model (string) — HuggingFace model identifier or local path for continual pretraining or SBERT fine-tuning. When set, model_class and model are not required (the architecture is inferred from the checkpoint).

  • tokenizer (object) — Tokenizer configuration, available to both the base_model path and custom from-scratch models. Two modes are selected via source: hf_repo (default) loads a pretrained tokenizer from name_or_path; train_from_dataset trains a new tokenizer from the dataset text (see §13.4). Required when using base_model with the mlm task.

  • model_class (enum) — Model architecture variant: frankenstein_text_encoder (mixed-architecture encoder), frankenstein_text_decoder (autoregressive causal decoder), or frankenstein_vit (vision transformer). Required when base_model is not set.

  • model (object) — Model architecture parameters (see §13.2). Required when base_model is not set.

  • training (object, required) — Training configuration (see §13.3).

The schema enforces a mutual-exclusivity rule: either base_model must be present, or both model_class and model must be present.

Model Configuration

The model object defines all architectural hyperparameters. Required fields are dims.vocab_size, dims.hidden_size, dims.num_layers, dims.num_heads, and dims.layer_pattern. Table 2 lists all model fields with their types and descriptions.

Complete model configuration fields. All fields are optional unless marked required.
Field Type Description
Field Type Description
dims.mode enum (encoder, decoder) Attention masking mode. encoder = bidirectional; decoder = causal.
dims.vocab_size int \(\ge 1\) (required) Number of unique tokens in the vocabulary. Must match the tokenizer’s vocab size.
dims.hidden_size int \(\ge 1\) (required) Hidden dimension. Must be divisible by num_heads. Typical: 512–2048.
dims.num_layers int \(\ge 1\) (required) Number of physical transformer layers. Typical: 6–24.
dims.num_loops int \(\ge 1\) Logical loop count. Each layer in layer_pattern runs num_loops times. Default: 1.
dims.num_heads int \(\ge 1\) (required) Number of parallel attention heads. Must divide hidden_size evenly.
dims.dropout float [0,1] Global dropout rate. Typical: 0.1 (BERT standard).
dims.layer_pattern array of enum (required) Ordered sequence of layer types. Length must equal num_layers. 47 mixer codes available (see Table 13.2.1).
norm.type enum Normalization strategy: layer_norm, dynamic_tanh, derf, rms_norm, prms_norm, flash_norm.
norm.partial_ratio float (0,1] Fraction of hidden dims for pRMSNorm estimation. Default: 0.0625.
embedding.factorized.enabled bool Enable embedding matrix factorization to reduce parameters.
embedding.factorized.dim int \(\ge 1\) Intermediate dimension for factorized embeddings. Typical: 64–256.
embedding.conv.enabled bool Apply Conv1d over token embeddings to capture local n-gram patterns.
embedding.conv.kernel int \(\ge 1\) Kernel size for embedding Conv1d. Typical: 3.
attention.ode.solver enum (rk4, euler) Numerical integration method for ODE layers. Default: rk4.
attention.ode.steps int \(\ge 1\) Integration steps between consecutive transformer layers. Default: 2.
attention.retnet.heads int \(\ge 1\) Retention heads for retnet/retnet layers. Must divide hidden_size. Default: 8.
attention.mla.latent_rank int \(\ge 1\) Rank of joint KV latent for MLA. Default: hidden_size // 2.
attention.gqla.latent_rank int \(\ge 1\) Rank of joint KV latent for GQLA. Default: hidden_size // 2.
attention.gqla.num_groups int \(\ge 1\) Number of GQA groups for GQLA decode path. Must divide num_heads.
attention.gqla.decode_path enum (mqa_absorb, gqa) Decoding path for GQLA.
attention.mlra.latent_rank int \(\ge 1\) Total latent rank for MLRA. Default: hidden_size // 2.
attention.mlra.num_latent_heads int \(\ge 1\) Number of disjoint latent sub-spaces for MLRA. Default: 4.
attention.tucker.query_rank int \(\ge 1\) Tucker rank for query weight tensor. Default: hidden_size.
attention.tucker.key_rank int \(\ge 1\) Tucker rank for key weight tensor. Default: hidden_size // 2.
attention.tucker.value_rank int \(\ge 1\) Tucker rank for value weight tensor. Default: hidden_size // 2.
attention.iha.num_pseudo_heads int \(\ge 1\) Number of pseudo-heads per head for IHA. Default: num_heads.
attention.gta.num_shared_groups int \(\ge 1\) Number of head groups sharing an attention map for GTA. Must divide num_heads.
attention.gta.value_latent_rank int \(\ge 1\) Rank of value-cache latent for GTA. Default: hidden_size // 2.
attention.mtla.latent_rank int \(\ge 1\) Latent rank for MTLA. Default: hidden_size // 2.
attention.mtla.merge_factor int \(\ge 1\) Number of consecutive KV entries merged per temporal slot. Default: 2.
attention.mtla.stride int \(\ge 1\) Stride between merged temporal slots. Default: mtla_merge_factor.
attention.cca.latent_rank int \(\ge 1\) Latent width for CCA. Default: hidden_size // 4. Must be divisible by num_heads.
attention.cca.num_conv_layers enum (0, 1, 2) Number of convolution layers in CCA. Default: 2.
attention.cca.conv_kernel_seq int \(\ge 1\) Kernel size of depth-wise causal sequence conv. Default: 4.
attention.cca.conv_kernel_ch int \(\ge 1\) Kernel size of head-wise grouped channel conv. Default: 3.
attention.cca.qk_mean bool Enable q-k-mean bias in CCA. Default: true.
attention.cca.value_shift bool Enable value-shift in CCA. Default: true.
attention.ccgqa.query_latent_rank int \(\ge 1\) Query latent width for CCGQA. Default: hidden_size // 2.
attention.ccgqa.kv_latent_rank int \(\ge 1\) KV latent width for CCGQA. Default: hidden_size // 8.
attention.ccgqa.num_kv_heads int \(\ge 1\) Number of KV heads for CCGQA. Must divide num_heads.
attention.ccgqa.num_conv_layers enum (0, 1, 2) Number of convolution layers in CCGQA. Default: 2.
attention.ccgqa.conv_kernel_seq int \(\ge 1\) Kernel size of depth-wise causal sequence conv. Default: 4.
attention.ccgqa.conv_kernel_ch int \(\ge 1\) Kernel size of head-wise grouped channel conv. Default: 3.
attention.ccgqa.qk_mean bool Enable q-k-mean bias in CCGQA. Default: true.
attention.ccgqa.value_shift bool Enable value-shift in CCGQA. Default: true.
attention.msa.block_size int \(\ge 1\) Block size for MiniMax Sparse Attention. Default: 128.
attention.msa.topk_blocks int \(\ge 1\) Number of blocks selected per GQA group per query. Default: 16.
attention.msa.index_dim int \(\ge 1\) Dimensionality of Index Branch heads. Default: 64.
attention.msa.kl_loss_weight float \(\ge 0\) Weight of KL alignment loss for MSA index branch. Default: 0.0.
attention.sparda.block_size int \(\ge 1\) KV block size for SparDA. Default: 128.
attention.sparda.topk_blocks int \(\ge 1\) Number of KV blocks selected per GQA group. Default: 16.
attention.sparda.forecast_dim int \(\ge 1\) Dimensionality of Forecast projection. Default: 64.
attention.lsa.num_long_range int \(\ge 1\) Long-range key budget \(k\) selected per query. Default: 2048.
attention.lsa.num_buckets int \(\ge 1\) Buckets scored per query \(p\); raised so \(p\cdot\)pool_size \(\ge k\). Default: 512.
attention.lsa.num_sinks int \(\ge 1\) Always-attended leading sink keys. Default: 4.
attention.lsa.pool_size int \(\ge 1\) Keys summed per pool key before Ward clustering. Default: 4.
attention.lsa.cluster_block int \(\ge 2\) Cluster block size; also the window \(n_w\). Default: 512.
attention.lsa.keys_per_bucket int \(\ge 1\) Average keys per bucket; yields cluster_block / keys_per_bucket buckets per block. Default: 8.
attention.lsa.max_keys_per_bucket int \(\ge 1\) Merge cap per bucket. Default: 16.
attention.fastconformer.window_size int \(\ge 2\) Total local span \(w\); per-side context \(w/2\) (paper: 128 each side). Default: 256.
attention.fastconformer.global_tokens int \(\ge 0\) Leading global attention tokens \(g\) (paper: 1; 0 = pure limited context). Default: 1.
attention.fastconformer.global_tokens_spacing int \(\ge 1\) Stride \(s\) between global positions \(\{0, s, \dots, (g{-}1)s\}\). Default: 1.
attention.fastconformer.global_attn_separate bool Separate global Q/K/V projections (\(+3H^2\); §2.2) vs shared (§3.4). Default: false.
attention.engram.max_ngram_size int \(\ge 2\) Maximum N-gram order for Engram memory module.
attention.engram.n_heads_per_ngram int \(\ge 1\) Number of hash heads per N-gram order.
attention.engram.embed_dim_per_head int \(\ge 1\) Embedding dimension per hash head.
attention.engram.kernel_size int \(\ge 1\) Causal depthwise conv kernel width for Engram.
attention.engram.seed int Random seed for N-gram hash multipliers.
mhc.enabled bool Enable the manifold-constrained n-stream residual (mHC, arXiv:2512.24880). Default: false.
mhc.expansion_rate int \(\ge 1\) Residual-stream expansion factor \(n\). The stream becomes \(n \times\) hidden_size. \(1\) recovers the identity mapping. Default: 4.
mhc.sinkhorn_iters int \(\ge 1\) Sinkhorn-Knopp normalisation rounds constraining \(H^{\text{res}}\) to be doubly stochastic. Default: 20.
mhc.gating_init float \(> 0\) Initial value of the mHC gating scalars \(\alpha\). Default: 0.01.
mhc.checkpoint bool Gradient checkpointing on mHC layers to mitigate the \(\sim n\times\) activation-memory increase. Default: false.
mhc.full_prec_under_bitnet bool Keep the mHC coefficient projection full-precision under BitNet. Default: true.
moe.enabled bool Enable Mixture of Experts in FFN layers. Default: true.
moe.num_experts int \(\ge 1\) Total number of expert networks. Default: 8.
moe.top_k int \(\ge 1\) Experts activated per token. Must be \(\le\) num_experts. Default: 2.
bitnet.enabled bool Enable BitLinear ternary weight quantization. Default: true.
bitnet.routers bool Also quantize routing/scoring projections. Requires bitnet.enabled=true. Default: false.
bitnet.conv bool Quantize embedding Conv1d with BitConv1d. Requires bitnet.enabled=true and embedding.conv.enabled=true. Default: false.
mixture_of_depths.enabled bool Enable Mixture-of-Depths token routing. Default: false.
mixture_of_depths.capacity_ratio float (0,1] Fraction of tokens updated per layer. Default: 0.5.
mixture_of_depths.router_aux_loss_weight float \(\ge 0\) Weight for the router auxiliary loss. Default: 0.0.
ssmax.enabled bool Enable Scalable Softmax (arXiv:2505.22842). Default: false.
ssmax.s_init float \(> 0\) Initial per-head SSMax scalar. Default: 1.0.
numerics.fixed_softmax bool Cancellation-free softmax/log-softmax (arXiv:2610.31642). Default: false.
numerics.fixed_cross_entropy bool Hard-target CE with zero-sum gradient by construction (arXiv:2610.31642). Default: false.
ffn.hidden_size int \(\ge 1\) Intermediate FFN dimension. Default: \(2\times\) hidden_size.
ffn.activation enum FFN non-linearity (43 values). Default: silu.
ffn.activation_config object Parameters for learnable/parametric activations.
classification_head.enabled bool Enable the NLP sequence-classification head. Default: false.
classification_head.num_labels int or null Number of classes.
classification_head.pooling_mode enum (cls, gap) Pooling for the classification head. Default: cls.

Fields are grouped under hierarchical sub-objects (dims, norm, embedding, attention, moe, bitnet, mixture_of_depths, ssmax, numerics, ffn, classification_head, mhc, residuals); each sub-header row marks the prefix in effect for the rows that follow it. There are no flat feature keys at model.*.

Layer Pattern Enumeration

The model.dims.layer_pattern array accepts the following 47 mixer codes. Each element defines one physical layer in the model stack. Table 3 lists all available types with their training and inference support.

Complete layer_pattern enumeration. \(\checkmark\) = supported, \(\times\) = not supported. fasa and sparge train as standard dense attention over their own projections and apply their sparse heuristic only at inference.
Type Description Train Infer
Type Description Train Infer
standard Classic multi-head self-attention (BERT-style)
sigmoid Sigmoid-gated attention
memory Memory Attention — token-ID memory values (V = K + Norm(E[s]))
gated_softmax Gated softmax attention with post-SDPA sigmoid
titan Titan attention with positional encoding (HoPE/RoPE)
retnet Retention Network (RNN+transformer hybrid)
mamba Selective state-space model (SSM)
ode Continuous-depth ODE layer
gla Gated Linear Attention with multiplicative decay
deltanet / gated_deltanet DeltaNet with corrective delta rule
gated_deltanet2 Gated DeltaNet-2 with decoupled channel-wise erase/write gates

Training Configuration

The training object controls the entire training pipeline. The only required field is task. Table 4 lists all training fields.

Complete training configuration fields.

Field Type Description

Tokenizer Configuration

The top-level tokenizer object is available to both training paths: the base_model route (continual pretraining / fine-tuning, where the tokenizer must match the pretrained checkpoint) and the custom from-scratch route (where it resolves the vocabulary before the embedding matrix is allocated). The source field selects between two modes:

  • hf_repo (default) — loads a pretrained tokenizer from name_or_path (a HuggingFace repo id or local path) through AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(). Complementary flags: use_fast (Rust-backed fast tokenizer, default true) and trust_remote_code (default false).

  • train_from_dataset — trains a new tokenizer from the corpus text with the HuggingFace tokenizers library. The corpus is the top-level text_dataset block (HF hub id, optionally streamed, or a local parquet/json directory); when the config is driven by an embedding host such as dashAI, the host’s run dataset can supply it instead. The resulting vocabulary size is injected into model.dims.vocab_size before model construction, so the embedding matrix always matches the tokenizer. In this mode name_or_path must be omitted.

Table 5 lists the tokenizer.training sub-object fields.

tokenizer.training.* fields (required when source=train_from_dataset).
Field Type Description
Field Type Description
algorithm enum (bpe, wordpiece, wordlevel, unigram) Tokenizer training algorithm. bpe (Byte Pair Encoding, GPT-2 style, default); wordpiece (original BERT); wordlevel (word lookup table); unigram (subword language model, auto-pruning).
vocab_size int \(\ge 1\) Target vocabulary size. Required for bpe/wordpiece/wordlevel; optional for unigram.
min_frequency int \(\ge 1\) Minimum token frequency to keep (default 2).
special_tokens array of string Special tokens registered in the tokenizer (default [PAD]/[UNK]/[CLS]/[SEP]/[MASK]).
save_dir string Directory persisted via save_pretrained().
lowercase bool Lowercase all text before training (default false).
strip_accents bool Strip diacritics before training (default false).
pre_tokenizer enum (whitespace, bytelevel, bert) Pre-tokenization strategy (default whitespace).
max_token_length int \(\ge 0\) Per-token character cap; 0 disables the limit.

Optimizer Configuration

The training.optimizer object has two fields:

  • optimizer_class (enum, required) — One of 23 optimizer algorithms: sgd_momentum, adamw, adafactor, galore_adamw, prodigy, lion, sophia, muon, turbo_muon, radam, adan, adopt, ademamix, mars_adamw, cautious_adamw, lamb, schedulefree_adamw, shampoo, soap, anon, apollo, apollo_mini, q_apollo.

  • parameters (object) — Optimizer hyperparameters with prefixed keys in the format <optimizer>-<group>_<param>.

Shared Per-Group Suffixes

All optimizers support the following per-parameter-group suffixes, prefixed by the optimizer class name (e.g., adamw-lr_embeddings):

  • Learning rate groups: lr_embeddings, lr_norms, lr_attention, lr_other

  • Weight decay groups: wd_embeddings, wd_norms, wd_attention, wd_other

  • Beta groups: betas_embeddings, betas_norms, betas_attention, betas_other

  • Epsilon groups: eps_embeddings, eps_norms, eps_attention, eps_other

Note: parameters of ODE, RetNet, and Mamba mixers are routed into the attention group rather than having dedicated groups.

Optimizer-Specific Global Suffixes

Table 6 lists the additional global suffixes supported by each optimizer (prefixed by the optimizer name).
