This annex collects the implementation-level detail for normalization variants, BitNet-style ternary quantization, adaptive depth routing (Mixture-of-Depths), conditional memory (Engram), factorized embeddings, and the runtime algorithms (training-step stability controls, SBERT inference router) that support the configuration-driven pipeline. (The manifold-constrained residual connections of mHC are documented separately in Annex 9.) The main sections defer to this annex for the mathematical formulations and pseudocode; the bibliography keys cited here resolve against docs/bibliography/.

Normalization Variants: LayerNorm, RMSNorm, pRMSNorm, Dynamic Tanh, Dynamic Erf, and FlashNorm

Normalization determines how activation scale is controlled across depth. In this repository, normalization is not only a modeling choice but also a schema compatibility question, because only certain values are currently accepted by norm_type. The schema contract is: \[\texttt{norm\_\allowbreak type} \in \{\texttt{layer\_\allowbreak norm}, \texttt{dynamic\_\allowbreak tanh}, \texttt{derf}, \texttt{rms\_\allowbreak norm}, \texttt{prms\_\allowbreak norm}, \texttt{flash\_\allowbreak norm}\}\] The formulations most relevant to this codebase are:

LayerNorm (Baseline)

LayerNorm is the default normalizer; it centers and rescales each token by its per-token mean and variance: \[\mu = \frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d} x_i, \quad \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}(x_i - \mu)^2, \quad y_i = \gamma_i \frac{x_i - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta_i.\]

RMSNorm

RMSNorm removes mean-centering and only rescales by root mean square magnitude : \[\mathrm{RMS}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i^2+\epsilon},\qquad y_i=\gamma_i\frac{x_i}{\mathrm{RMS}(x)}.\] Compared with LayerNorm, RMSNorm is computationally simpler (no subtraction of feature mean) and is often used when reducing normalization overhead is important (e.g., Llama, GPT-NeoX). It has a learnable per-dimension scale \(\gamma\) but no bias term.

Partial RMSNorm (pRMSNorm)

pRMSNorm further reduces overhead by estimating the RMS from only the first \(p\)% of the hidden dimensions: \[\mathrm{RMS}(x)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_i^2+\epsilon},\qquad k=\lceil d\cdot p\rceil,\] exploiting the assumption that neurons within a layer are approximately i.i.d. The same scale \(\gamma\) is then applied to all dimensions. The partial ratio \(p\) is controlled by the prms_partial_ratio config field (default \(6.25\%\)). The paper reports that competitive results are achievable with as little as \(6.25\%\) of the inputs, though gradient instability can arise with very small ratios.

Dynamic Tanh (DyT)

Dynamic Tanh proposes replacing explicit normalization with a bounded elementwise map : \[\mathrm{DyT}(x)=\tanh(\alpha x)\] where \(\alpha\) is learned. The core idea is that bounded nonlinear contraction can provide stable signal scaling without explicitly computing per-token normalization statistics.

Dynamic Erf (Derf)

Derf extends the same normalization-free direction by using an error-function based map : \[\mathrm{Derf}(x)=\mathrm{erf}(\alpha x+s)\] with learnable scale/shift. Reported results in the cited work indicate stronger performance than DyT and common normalization baselines across multiple domains.

FlashNorm (Weightless RMSNorm)

FlashNorm is not a new mathematical normalization; it is an exact algebraic rewrite of the ubiquitous “\(\mathrm{RMSNorm} \to \mathrm{Linear}\)” pair that (i) eliminates the per-dimension learnable scale \(\mathbf{g}\) by folding it into the subsequent linear layer’s weights, and (ii) defers the scalar RMS reduction to the output of the matrix multiplication so that the matmul (matrix unit) and the RMS reduction (vector unit) execute in parallel. Three propositions formalize the rewrite.

Proposition 1 (Weight folding).

Given activation \(\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), RMSNorm weight \(\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), and a subsequent linear \(\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\), \[\mathbf{z}=\mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathbf{a})\mathbf{W}=\frac{\mathbf{a}}{\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{a})}\mathbf{W}^{*},\qquad W^{*}_{i,j}=g_{i}\cdot W_{i,j}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \mathbf{W}^{*}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{g})\mathbf{W}.\] The per-dimension scale \(\mathbf{g}\) becomes redundant and is folded into \(\mathbf{W}\) once at load time. The standalone FlashNorm module in this repository applies this directly: it has no learnable parameters (the scale is meant to be absorbed by the downstream projection).

Proposition 2 (Deferred normalization).

For a bias-free linear \(\mathbf{W}^{*}\), scalar–matrix commutativity yields \[\frac{\mathbf{a}}{\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{a})}\mathbf{W}^{*}=\left(\mathbf{a}\mathbf{W}^{*}\right)\cdot\frac{1}{\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{a})}.\] The matmul \(\mathbf{a}\mathbf{W}^{*}\) and the RMS reduction are independent of each other; on hardware with distinct matrix and vector execution units they execute in parallel, and only a single vector–scalar multiply synchronizes them. The fused module FlashNormLinear implements this rewrite: on the bias-free path it computes the matmul on the un-normalized input and multiplies the result by the per-token reciprocal RMS. When the linear has a bias \(\mathbf{c}\), the rewrite is no longer exact (Remark 1 of the paper): \(\left(\mathbf{a}\mathbf{W}^{*}+\mathbf{c}\right)/\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{a})\neq\mathbf{a}\mathbf{W}^{*}/\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{a})+\mathbf{c}\); the layer then applies the scalar to the input first and lets the linear add its bias as usual.

Proposition 3 (RMS cancellation).

By RMS scale invariance, \(\mathrm{RMS}(\alpha\mathbf{a})=\alpha\,\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{a})\). Therefore an “\(\mathrm{RMSNorm}\to\mathrm{Linear}\to\mathrm{RMSNorm}\)” pattern allows the first RMSNorm to be dropped entirely: \[\mathrm{RMSNorm}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{a}}{\mathrm{RMS}(\mathbf{a})}\mathbf{W}^{*}\right)=\mathrm{RMSNorm}\!\left(\mathbf{a}\mathbf{W}^{*}\right).\] This cancellation is relevant for QKV-normalization (Gemma 4) and MLA latent normalization (DeepSeek-V2, Mistral Small 4); it is not auto-applied in this repository but is documented for completeness.

Partial-RMS composition.

FlashNorm composes naturally with the pRMSNorm trick (§20, pRMSNorm subsection): when flashnorm_partial_ratio \(=p>0\), the RMS is estimated from the first \(k=\lceil d\cdot p\rceil\) dimensions of the input only, reducing the cost of the vector-unit RMS reduction further.

BitNet interaction.

Folding a floating-point \(\mathbf{g}\) into BitNet’s ternary weight tensor \(\{-1,0,+1\}\) would destroy the quantization, and BitLinear applies its own internal LayerNorm before activation quantization which needs the normalized input. The fused module FlashNormBitLinear therefore falls back to the sequential composition \(\mathrm{FlashNorm}\to\mathrm{BitLinear}\): the matmul and the RMS reduction still execute in parallel, but the post-matmul scalar multiply of Prop. 2 is sacrificed. Folding f.p. \(\mathbf{g}\) into a 1.58-bit weight tensor is left to future kernel-level work.

PyTorch pseudocode.

Input: activation \(\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times n}\), RMSNorm weight \(\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), linear \(\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\), bias \(\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{k}\) or None // Prop. 1: weight folding at load time \(\mathbf{W}^{*}\gets \mathbf{g}\odot\mathbf{W}\) \(\mathbf{g}\gets \mathbf{1}\) // Prop. 2: forward pass with deferred RMS (bias-free path) \(\mathbf{b}\gets \mathbf{a}\mathbf{W}^{*\top}\) \(\mathrm{rms\_\allowbreak inv}\gets \mathrm{rsqrt}(\mathrm{mean}(\mathbf{a}^{2})+\varepsilon)\) return \(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathrm{rms\_\allowbreak inv}\) // Remark 1: bias path is sequential; matmul and RMS still parallelize return \((\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathrm{rms\_\allowbreak inv})\mathbf{W}^{*\top}+\mathbf{c}\)

Query–Key Normalization and Attention-Logit Control

Attention logits \(\ell_{i,t,h} = \mathbf{q}_{i,h}^\top \mathbf{k}_{t,g(h)} / \sqrt{d_h}\) are the input to the softmax. Their unbounded growth is a canonical source of training instability: saturated attention, entropy collapse, loss spikes and, at scale, divergence . This repository exposes five mechanisms under norm.qk_norm.method; three act in the forward pass and two act on the optimizer state. They are mutually exclusive per configuration.

Forward-time QK normalization.

QK normalization normalizes queries and keys along the per-head feature dimension before the dot product. In RMSNorm form, \[\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{i,h} = \frac{\mathbf{q}'_{i,h}\odot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_q}{S_q(\mathbf{q}'_{i,h})},\qquad S_q(\mathbf{q}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{d_h}\sum_{j=1}^{d_h} q_j^2 + \epsilon},\] and identically for \(\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) with \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_k\). The affine weights are shared across heads and broadcast over the head axis, so the parameter cost is \(2d_h\) (rms_norm) or \(2\cdot 2d_h\) with bias (layer_norm); l2_norm is weightless. Because the normalized norms satisfy \(\|\hat{\mathbf{q}}\|_2 \approx \|\boldsymbol{\gamma}_q\|_2\) up to direction and \(\epsilon\), the residual logit growth is mediated by the learned affine product \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}_q\odot\boldsymbol{\gamma}_k\) rather than by uncontrolled raw query/key norms.

QK normalization with Multi-Head Latent Attention.

MLA caches a low-rank latent \(\mathbf{c}_t\) and reconstructs keys by up-projection, so post-projection QK RMSNorm appears to require the full keys that MLA avoids caching. show the incompatibility is an implementation artifact: RMSNorm decomposes into a static affine weight and a dynamic scalar statistic, \[\hat{\mathbf{k}}^c_{t,g}=\frac{(\mathbf{c}_t\mathbf{W}^K_g)\odot\boldsymbol{\gamma}^c_k}{S^c_k(\mathbf{c}_t\mathbf{W}^K_g)},\qquad \ell^c_{i,t,h}=\big((\mathbf{q}'^{c}_{i,h}\odot\boldsymbol{\gamma}^c_q\odot\boldsymbol{\gamma}^c_k)(\mathbf{W}^K_{g(h)})^\top\big)\cdot\mathbf{c}_t\;\alpha^q_{i,h}\alpha^k_{t,g(h)},\] where \(\alpha^q=1/S_q\) and \(\alpha^k=1/S_k\) are scalars. The static weight is absorbed into the query-side projection and only one inverse-RMS scalar per token and KV group is cached (\(T\times G\) scalars versus \(T\times G\times d_c\) full content keys), which keeps MLA’s latent decode path intact; the paper reports lower loss than QK-Clip and \(<2\%\) decode overhead up to 256k tokens. In this repository the MLA variant of already re-expands keys from the cached latent on every step, so explicit per-head normalization of the decompressed \(\mathbf{q}\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) is exactly equivalent to the absorbed formulation in both training and cached decoding; no scalar cache is required. Content and RoPE blocks are normalized blockwise, matching the natural boundary between the latent content path and the small materialized rotary path.

QK-Clip.

Kimi K2’s MuonClip targets the same failure mode after the dot product. For each head \(h\) it defines the per-head maximum pre-softmax logit over the batch, \[S^h_{\max}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\max_{\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{B}}\max_{i,j}\mathbf{Q}^h_i{\mathbf{K}^h_j}^\top,\] and, after every optimizer step, rescales the projection weights with \[\gamma_h=\min\!\left(1,\frac{\tau}{S^h_{\max}}\right),\qquad \mathbf{W}^h_q\leftarrow\gamma_h^{\alpha}\mathbf{W}^h_q,\qquad \mathbf{W}^h_k\leftarrow\gamma_h^{1-\alpha}\mathbf{W}^h_k .\] The intervention never alters the current forward/backward pass; heads already below \(\tau\) receive \(\gamma_h=1\), so the mechanism self-deactivates once training stabilizes (K2 used \(\tau=100\) and observed all heads below threshold after roughly 30% of steps). We apply it per head to the row blocks of q_proj and k_proj; for latent attention the key side is uk_proj, and for grouped-query attention each KV head receives the smallest \(\gamma_h\) of the query heads that read it, which bounds every logit in the group. clip_alpha defaults to \(0.5\) (i.e. \(\sqrt{\gamma_h}\) on each side, the balanced K2 choice).

QuacK.

Instead of a forward or weight intervention, QuacK assigns parameter-dependent learning rates to the query and key weights. Storing the Frobenius norms at initialization, before each step it sets \[\eta_{W_Q}=\tau\,\eta\,\frac{\|\mathbf{W}_K\|_{\mathrm{init}}}{\|\mathbf{W}_K\|},\qquad \eta_{W_K}=\tau\,\eta\,\frac{\|\mathbf{W}_Q\|_{\mathrm{init}}}{\|\mathbf{W}_Q\|},\] which follows from controlling the first-order change \(\Delta\ell\approx(\mathbf{q}\,\Delta\mathbf{k}^\top+\Delta\mathbf{q}\,\mathbf{k}^\top)/\sqrt{d}\): when one side grows, the learning rate of the other decreases. Frobenius and spectral norms performed indistinguishably in the paper, so Frobenius is used. The relative rate \(\tau\) defaults to \(1.0\); the paper reports stability comparable to QK-norm at high base learning rates and about a 10% speedup because two RMS reductions per block disappear. The mechanism is optimizer-agnostic here: the trainer splits the query/key weights into dedicated parameter groups, so any registered optimizer can carry it.

Schema contract and validation.

norm.qk_norm is a sub-object with enabled, method \(\in\) {rms_norm, layer_norm, l2_norm, qk_clip, quack}, clip_tau, clip_alpha, quack_tau and eps. The mechanism requires explicit per-head query/key projections: enabling it for a layer pattern containing a recurrent or state-space mixer is rejected at load time (QK_NORM_MIXERS); qk_clip additionally requires per-head dot-product logits and therefore excludes the Gaussian-mixture router (QK_CLIP_MIXERS).

PyTorch pseudocode (QK-Clip).

Input: model, threshold \(\tau\), exponent \(\alpha\), cached per-head \(S^h_{\max}\) \(\gamma_h\gets\tau/S^h_{\max}\) \(\mathbf{W}^h_q\gets\gamma_h^{\alpha}\mathbf{W}^h_q\) \(\mathbf{W}^h_k\gets\gamma_h^{1-\alpha}\mathbf{W}^h_k\) clear \(S^h_{\max}\)

Comparison.

L2.1cmL3.5cmL2.4cmL4.3cm Method & Intervention & Extra state & Notes
rms_norm & per-head forward RMSNorm & \(2d_h\) & Standard QK-norm; exact with this repo’s re-expanding MLA .
layer_norm & per-head forward LayerNorm & \(4d_h\) & Mean-centering variant (SAN); slightly heavier.
l2_norm & per-head forward L2 & none & Weightless ablation.

BitNet Ternary Quantization Path

When use_bitnet=true, BitLinear layers replace standard nn.Linear with ternary weight quantization (\(-1, 0, +1\)) following BitNet . Given weight tensor \(W\), a practical scaling is: \[s=\text{mean}(|W|),\qquad \tilde{W}=\text{clip}\left(\text{round}\left(\frac{W}{s}\right),-1,1\right).\] The packed mapping uses two bits per weight symbol for storage efficiency. This enables significant compression (\(\sim 32\times\) versus FP32) but is experimental and may affect model quality; it is best suited for inference deployment.

Activation quantization for the INT8 path is: \[q=\text{round}\left(x\cdot\frac{127}{\max(|x|)+\epsilon}\right),\qquad q\in[-128,127]\] with dequantization \(x\approx q/\alpha\). For \(N\) parameters, size estimates before metadata and packing overhead are: \[\text{FP32 size}\approx 4N,\quad \text{FP16 size}\approx 2N,\quad \text{1.58-bit size}\approx \frac{1.58}{8}N\] which aligns with lightweight deployment goals .

Mixture-of-Depths (MoD) Token Routing

When use_mixture_of_depths=true, each transformer block scores tokens with a lightweight router. Only the top mixture_of_depths_capacity_ratio subset is updated; skipped tokens pass through unchanged . This allocates more depth to salient tokens, reducing per-layer compute.

Input: hidden states \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\), router \(R\), capacity ratio \(\rho\) \(\text{scores} \gets R(H)\) \(\mathcal{S} \gets \texttt{top-k}(\text{scores}, k=\lceil \rho \cdot n \rceil)\) \(H_{\text{update}} \gets \texttt{block}(H[\mathcal{S}])\) \(H[\mathcal{S}] \gets H_{\text{update}}\) Output: \(H\)

Configuration

  • use_mixture_of_depths: bool — enable MoD token routing.

  • mixture_of_depths_capacity_ratio: float in \((0, 1]\) — fraction of tokens updated per layer.

  • mixture_of_depths_router_aux_loss_weight: float \(\ge 0\) — auxiliary loss weight for router regularization.

Engram Conditional Memory

Engram (engram) implements conditional memory via scalable N-gram lookup . It builds hash-based lookup tables for N-gram contexts from size 2 up to engram_max_ngram_size, with independent hash heads per N-gram order. A causal depthwise convolution (engram_kernel_size) provides short-range context before the N-gram lookup.

Input: token stream \(x_{1:n}\), N-gram orders \(\{2, \ldots, N\}\), hash heads per order \(H\) \(h_{\text{conv}} \gets \text{DepthwiseConv1d}(x_{1:n}, k=\texttt{engram\_\allowbreak kernel\_\allowbreak size})\) \(\text{ctx}_t^{(k)} \gets x_{t-k+1:t}\) \(\text{lookup}^{(k)}_t \gets \text{HashTable}^{(k)}[\text{hash}(\text{ctx}_t^{(k)})]\) \(y_t \gets \sum_{k} \text{lookup}^{(k)}_t + h_{\text{conv},t}\) Output: \(y_{1:n}\)

Configuration

  • engram_max_ngram_size: int \(\ge 2\) — highest N-gram order (default 3).

  • engram_n_heads_per_ngram: int \(\ge 1\) — hash heads per N-gram order (default 4).

  • engram_embed_dim_per_head: int \(\ge 1\) — embedding dim per hash head (default 32).

  • engram_kernel_size: int \(\ge 1\) — causal depthwise conv kernel width (default 4).

  • engram_seed: int — hash seed for reproducibility (default 42).

Total Engram hidden size = \((\texttt{max\_\allowbreak ngram\_\allowbreak size} - 1) \times \texttt{n\_\allowbreak heads\_\allowbreak per\_\allowbreak ngram} \times \texttt{embed\_\allowbreak dim\_\allowbreak per\_\allowbreak head}\).

Factorized Embeddings and Embedding Convolution

Factorized Embeddings

When use_factorized_embedding=true, the embedding matrix is factorized into two smaller matrices, reducing parameters from \(O(V \times H)\) to \(O(V \times R + R \times H)\) where \(R = \texttt{factorized\_\allowbreak embedding\_\allowbreak dim}\).

  • use_factorized_embedding: bool — enable factorization.

  • factorized_embedding_dim: int \(\ge 1\) — intermediate dimension (typical: 64–256).

Embedding Convolution

When use_embedding_conv=true, a depthwise Conv1d is applied over the embedding stream before the first transformer block, with kernel size embedding_conv_kernel. This provides a lightweight local-context filter on token embeddings.

Training-Step Stability Controls

The schema-driven training step applies gradient accumulation, global-norm clipping, post-clip explosion guards, and bounded NaN/Inf retries. The accumulated gradient is: \[g_{\text{acc}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K} g_i,\quad K=\texttt{gradient\_\allowbreak accumulation\_\allowbreak steps}\] \[g_{\text{clip}} = g_{\text{acc}}\cdot \min\left(1,\frac{\tau}{\|g_{\text{acc}}\|_2+\epsilon}\right),\quad \tau=\texttt{grad\_\allowbreak clip\_\allowbreak max\_\allowbreak norm}\] then overflow guards use inf_post_clip_threshold and retry logic bounded by max_nan_retries.

Batch stream, config \(C\) Initialize retry counter \(r\gets 0\) Accumulate gradients for \(K=C.\texttt{gradient\_\allowbreak accumulation\_\allowbreak steps}\) micro-batches Apply global norm clipping with \(\tau=C.\texttt{grad\_\allowbreak clip\_\allowbreak max\_\allowbreak norm}\) restore safe state / skip step; \(r \gets r+1\) continue stop training with failure state run optimizer step selected by optimizer_class update scheduler (cosine, constant, or linear_warmup_then_constant) save rolling checkpoint and prune to max_rolling_checkpoints update best checkpoints up to num_best_checkpoints emit CSV + telemetry following gradient_log_interval and telemetry_log_interval

Held-Out Test Split and End-of-Training Evaluation

training.test_percentage reserves a deterministic fraction of the task dataset before the first optimizer step. With \(n\) dataset examples, held-out percentage \(\rho=\texttt{test\_\allowbreak percentage}/100\), and a permutation \(\pi\) drawn once from the run seed training.seed, the partition is \[n_{\text{test}}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\operatorname{round}(\rho n),\,1,\,n-1\right),\qquad \mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}=\{x_{\pi(i)}\}_{i=n_{\text{test}}+1}^{n},\qquad \mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}=\{x_{\pi(i)}\}_{i=1}^{n_{\text{test}}} ,\] so the same configuration always reserves the same examples regardless of DataLoader shuffling. After the last epoch the final weights are evaluated once with the task objective under no_grad, and the sample-weighted loss and accuracy \[\hat{L}=\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}}\ell(f_\theta;x),\qquad \widehat{\text{acc}}=\frac{1}{n_{\text{test}}}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}}a(f_\theta;x)\] are written to test_metrics.json next to the CSV log. The split covers masked and causal language modeling, text classification, the three vision tasks, ASR (where the accuracy slot carries the character error rate, labelled metric: cer), and audio classification. SBERT keeps its own validation partition through training.sbert.max_eval_samples and is unaffected. Setting the field to zero disables the split and restores the historical all-data behavior.

SBERT Inference Mode Router

The SBERT inference dispatcher selects among similarity scoring, corpus search, clustering, and persistent encoding modes over a single shared encoder . The cosine similarity and regression loss are: \[\text{cos}(e_1,e_2)=\frac{e_1^\top e_2}{\|e_1\|\|e_2\|},\qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{cos}}=\left(\text{cos}(e_1,e_2)-y\right)^2\] with \(y\in[-1,1]\) in this pipeline.

mode \(m\), model \(E\), inputs \(X\) return \(\cos(E(x_1),E(x_2))\) return top-\(k\) by dot-product/cosine against corpus embeddings return clustering labels over \(E(X)\) return serialized embeddings \(E(X)\)

Activation Functions

This annex documents the complete activation-function library available in the model. The library provides 43 feed-forward activation functions: 40 elementwise activations and 3 gated-FFN variants. Activations are grouped into five families, following the taxonomy of Dubey et al.  and the analytic overview of Lederer , augmented with the learnable Rational Activation Function (RAF) of Fang et al. .

The selection is driven by the ffn_activation configuration field (a string enum) and dispatched at runtime by a factory function that mirrors the normalization-layer dispatch (Annex 7).

\[\texttt{ffn\_\allowbreak activation} \in \{\texttt{silu},\;\texttt{gelu},\;\dots,\; \texttt{raf},\;\texttt{swiglu},\;\texttt{geglu},\;\texttt{reglu}\}\]

Classical / Sigmoid–Tanh Family (12 activations)

The classical family comprises smooth, stateless activations rooted in logistic and algebraic functions . All share monotonicity or near-monotonicity and are continuously differentiable.

\[\begin{aligned} \text{Sigmoid}(x) &= \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} & \text{Range: } (0,1),\;\text{monotonic, smooth} & \quad \text{\citep{lederer2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{Tanh}(x) &= \frac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{e^{x}+e^{-x}} = 2\,\sigma(2x)-1 & \text{Range: } (-1,1),\;\text{monotonic, smooth} & \quad \text{\citep{lederer2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{Arctan}(x) &= \arctan(x) & \text{Range: } (-\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{\pi}{2}),\;\text{monotonic, smooth} & \quad \text{\citep{lederer2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{Softsign}(x) &= \frac{x}{1+|x|} & \text{Range: } (-1,1),\;\text{smooth, once-diff.\ at 0} & \quad \text{\citep{lederer2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{Elliott}(x) &= \frac{x}{1+|x|} & \text{Alias of Softsign (survey ``elliottsig'' notation)} & \quad \text{\citep{lederer2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{Identity}(x) &= x & \text{Range: } (-\infty,\infty),\;\text{linear, }C^\infty & \quad \text{(internal)} \end{aligned}\]

\[\begin{aligned} \text{Softplus}(x) &= \log(1+e^{x}) & \text{Range: } [0,\infty),\;\text{smooth, }C^\infty & \quad \text{\citep{glorot2011softplus}} \\[4pt] \text{Mish}(x) &= x\,\tanh\!\big(\text{softplus}(x)\big) = x\,\tanh\!\big(\log(1+e^{x})\big) & \text{Range: } [\approx{-0.31},\infty),\;\text{non-monotonic, smooth} & \quad \text{\citep{misra2019mish}} \\[4pt] \text{GELU}(x) &= x\,\Phi(x) = x\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\Big(1+\text{erf}\!\Big(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\Big)\Big) & \text{Range: } (\approx{-0.17},\infty),\;\text{smooth, probabilistic} & \quad \text{\citep{hendrycks2016gelu}} \\[4pt] \text{GELU-tanh}(x) &= \tfrac{x}{2}\Big(1+\tanh\!\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{\pi}} (x+0.044715\,x^{3})\Big)\Big) & \text{Tanh approximation of GELU (faster)} & \quad \text{\citep{hendrycks2016gelu}} \\[4pt] \text{ReLU}(x) &= \max(0,x) & \text{Range: } [0,\infty),\;\text{piecewise-linear, non-smooth at 0} & \quad \text{\citep{nair2010relu}} \\[4pt] \text{SiLU}(x) &= x\,\sigma(x) = \frac{x}{1+e^{-x}} & \text{Range: } (\approx{-0.278},\infty),\;\text{non-monotonic, smooth} & \quad \text{\citep{elfwing2018silu}} \end{aligned}\]

SiLU (Sigmoid Linear Unit) is the default activation (ffn_activation=silu). When \(\beta=1\), the parametric Swish reduces to SiLU. GELU and its tanh approximation are the standard in BERT and GPT-2/3 . Mish  is a self-regularized, non-monotonic composition of Softplus and Tanh, reported to outperform Swish on several benchmarks.

Rectified Family (12 activations)

The rectifier family extends ReLU with learnable slopes, bounded variants, and rectified-hyperbolic forms .

\[\begin{aligned} \text{LeakyReLU}(x) &= \begin{cases} x & x\ge 0 \\ a\,x & x < 0 \end{cases}, \quad a=0.01 & \text{Range: } (-\infty,\infty) & \quad \text{\citep{maas2013leakyrelu}} \\[4pt] \text{ReLU6}(x) &= \min\!\big(\max(0,x),\,6\big) & \text{Range: } [0,6],\;\text{bounded, fixed-point friendly} & \quad \text{\citep{howard2017mobile}} \\[4pt] \text{HardSwish}(x) &= x\cdot\frac{\text{ReLU6}(x+3)}{6} & \text{Range: } (\approx{-1.67},\infty),\;\text{cheap Swish approx.} & \quad \text{\citep{howard2019hardswish}} \\[4pt] \text{PReLU}(x) &= \max(0,x)+\mathbf{p}\odot\min(0,x) & \text{Learnable per-channel slope } \mathbf{p},\;\text{init 0.25} & \quad \text{\citep{he2015prelu}} \\[4pt] \text{AbsReLU}(x) &= \max(0,x)-\max(0,-x) = x\;\text{(sign-ramp)} & \text{Range: } (-\infty,\infty) & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{NLReLU}(x) &= \beta\,\log\!\big(1+\max(0,x)\big) & \text{Range: } [0,\infty),\;\beta=1.0,\;\text{logarithmic compression} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \end{aligned}\]

\[\begin{aligned} \text{BReLU}(x) &= \min\!\big(\max(0,x),\,t\big),\quad t=1.0 & \text{Range: } [0,t],\;\text{bounded rectifier} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{VReLU}(x) &= |x| & \text{Range: } [0,\infty),\;\text{symmetric rectifier} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{Hexpo}(x) &= a\,\max(0,x)-c\,\max(0,-x),\quad a{=}c{=}1.0 & \text{Asymmetric two-sided rectifier} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{PenalizedTanh}(x) &= \max\!\big(0,\,\tanh(x)\big) & \text{Range: } [0,1),\;\text{rectified tanh, smooth near 0} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{DisReLU}(x) &= \max(0,\,x-\delta),\quad \delta=0.0 & \text{Right-shifted ReLU hinge} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{LiSHT}(x) &= x\,\tanh(x) & \text{Range: } [0,\infty)\;\text{(magnitude), non-monotonic, smooth} & \quad \text{\citep{roy2019lisht}} \end{aligned}\]

PReLU  makes the negative slope a per-channel learnable parameter, enabling the network to learn the optimal leak per feature. HardSwish  is the cheap Swish approximation used in MobileNetV3. ReLU6  was introduced in MobileNetV1 for fixed-point quantization friendliness.

Exponential / ELU Family (12 activations)

The exponential-linear family provides smooth negative saturation and self-normalizing variants . Several members introduce per-channel learnable parameters.

\[\begin{aligned} \text{ELU}(x) &= \begin{cases} x & x\ge 0 \\ \alpha(e^{x}-1) & x<0 \end{cases}, \quad \alpha=1.0 & \text{Range: } (-\alpha,\infty) & \quad \text{\citep{clevert2016elu}} \\[4pt] \text{SELU}(x) &= \lambda\,\text{ELU}_{\alpha'}(x) & \alpha'{\approx}1.6733,\;\lambda{\approx}1.0507, & \quad \text{\citep{klambauer2017selu}} \\ & & \text{self-normalizing (mean 0, var 1)} & \notag \\[4pt] \text{CELU}(x) &= \begin{cases} x & x\ge 0 \\ \alpha(e^{x/\alpha}-1) & x<0 \end{cases}, \quad \alpha=1.0 & \text{Once-diff.\ at 0 for any } \alpha & \quad \text{\citep{barron2017celu}} \\[4pt] \text{PELU}(x) &= \begin{cases} \tfrac{\alpha}{\beta}\,x & x\ge 0 \\ \alpha(e^{x/\beta}-1) & x<0 \end{cases} & \alpha,\beta\text{ learnable per-channel} & \quad \text{\citep{trottier2017pelu}} \\[4pt] \text{MPELU}(x) &= \text{ReLU}(x)+\beta\cdot\text{ELU}_{\alpha}(x)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{x<0} & \alpha,\beta\text{ learnable per-channel} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \end{aligned}\]

\[\begin{aligned} \text{FELU}(x) &= \begin{cases} x & x\ge 0 \\ \alpha(e^{x}-1) & x<0 \end{cases} & \alpha\text{ learnable, clamped to } [0,1] & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{EELU}(x) &= \beta\,\text{ReLU}(x)+\alpha(e^{x}-1)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{x<0} & \alpha,\beta\text{ learnable per-channel} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{PDELU}(x) &= \begin{cases} x & x\ge 0 \\ \alpha(e^{x/\alpha}-1)+(1-\alpha)\,x & x<0 \end{cases} & \alpha\text{ learnable, interpolates CELU--identity} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{PREU}(x) &= \beta\,\text{ReLU}(x)+\alpha(e^{x}-1)\cdot\mathbb{1}_{x<0}^{\le 0} & \alpha,\beta\text{ learnable per-channel} & \quad \text{\citep{dubey2021activations}} \\[4pt] \text{SoftExp}(x) &= \begin{cases} \tfrac{1}{\alpha}\big(e^{\alpha x}-1\big)+\alpha & \alpha>0 \\ x & \alpha=0 \\ -\tfrac{1}{\alpha}\ln\!\big(1-\alpha(x+\alpha)\big) & \alpha<0 \end{cases} & \alpha\text{ learnable; exp/linear/log interpolation} & \quad \text{\citep{godfrey2015softexp}} \end{aligned}\]

\[\begin{aligned} \text{ELiSH}(x) &= \begin{cases} x\,\sigma(x) & x\ge 0 \\ (e^{x}-1)\,\sigma(x) & x<0 \end{cases} & \text{Swish pos.\ branch, ELU-gated neg.\ branch} & \quad \text{\citep{basirat2019elish}} \\[4pt] \text{HardELiSH}(x) &= \begin{cases} x\cdot\text{hard\_\allowbreak sigmoid}(x) & x\ge 0 \\ (e^{x}-1)\cdot\text{hard\_\allowbreak sigmoid}(x) & x<0 \end{cases} & \text{Hard-sigmoid variant of ELiSH} & \quad \text{\citep{basirat2019elish}} \end{aligned}\]

where \(\text{hard\_\allowbreak sigmoid}(x)=\text{ReLU6}(x+3)/6\).

ELU  provides smooth negative saturation. SELU  induces self-normalization with fixed \(\alpha'{\approx}1.6733\), \(\lambda{\approx}1.0507\). CELU  is once-differentiable at 0 for any \(\alpha\) (unlike ELU). PELU  makes both \(\alpha,\beta\) learnable per-channel. The parametric variants (MPELU, FELU, EELU, PDELU, PREU) generalize ELU and PReLU by introducing learnable per-channel parameters for the negative and positive branches. SoftExp  continuously interpolates between logarithmic (\(\alpha<0\)), linear (\(\alpha=0\)), and exponential (\(\alpha>0\)) regimes. ELiSH and HardELiSH  combine Swish and ELU behaviors via a piecewise definition.

Swish and Parametric Activations

Swish  is a family parameterized by a slope \(\beta\): \[\text{Swish}_\beta(x) = x\,\sigma(\beta x) = \frac{x}{1+e^{-\beta x}}.\] When \(\beta=1\) this is SiLU (the default). Large \(\beta\) approaches ReLU; \(\beta\to 0\) approaches the linear function \(x/2\).

  • Swish (swish): fixed \(\beta\) (default 1.0, configured via ffn_activation_config.swish_beta). No learnable parameters.

  • SwishTrainable (swish_trainable): \(\beta\) is a per-channel learnable parameter, initialized to 1.0. Equivalent to SiLU at initialization, then adapts during training.

  • Maxout (maxout): computes \(k\) linear projections and takes the elementwise maximum: \(\max_{i=0}^{k-1}(W_i x + b_i)\). A universal approximator for any continuous function given enough pieces. Parameter count increases by factor \(k\) (default \(k=2\), configured via ffn_activation_config.maxout_pieces).

References: Swish , Maxout .

Rational Activation Functions (RAF)

Following Fang et al. , a Rational Activation Function is a learnable ratio of two low-degree polynomials (a Padé approximant): \[F(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{m} a_j\, x^{j}} {1 + R(x)}\] where \(\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{m+1}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\) are learnable, and the denominator term \(R(x)\) depends on the version. The default configuration matches the paper: degree \((m,n)=(5,4)\), version “A” (safe), initialized by a least-squares fit to GELU on \([-3,3]\).

The implementation supports five denominator variants:

  • Version A (default, “safe”): \(Q(x)=1+\sum_{k}|b_k\, x^{k+1}|\) (per-term absolute value). Guarantees \(Q(x)\ge 1\), no division by zero.

  • Version B: \(Q(x)=1+\big|\sum_{k} b_k\, x^{k+1}\big|\) (absolute value of the whole sum). Also guarantees \(Q(x)\ge 1\).

  • Version C: \(Q(x)=0.1+\big|\sum_{k} b_k\, x^{k}\big|\) with a \(0.1\) floor. Minimum denominator \(0.1\).

  • Version D: like B, but injects uniform multiplicative noise \(U(1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon)\) on the denominator weights during training only (\(\varepsilon=0.1\)). Regularization effect.

  • Version N (“nunsafe”): \(Q(x)=1+\sum_{k} b_k\, x^{k+1}\) without any absolute value. Can have poles (denominator zeros); use with care.

RAFT input scaling. Because a Padé approximant is a reliable universal approximator only on a bounded interval, the RAFT model preprocesses each token’s pre-activations with a per-token min–max scaling into \([-3,3]\): \[\tilde{x} = \frac{x-\min(x)}{\max(x)-\min(x)}\cdot 6 - 3.\] This is toggled by ffn_activation_config.raf_input_scaling (default false).

Initialization targets. The rational coefficients can be initialized by fitting to any of the following target functions: gelu (default), relu, leaky_relu, leaky_relu_, sigmoid, tanh, swish/silu, or identity. The fit uses a least-squares solve on 2001 uniformly spaced samples over \([-3,3]\).

Freezing. Setting raf_trainable=false freezes the rational parameters, useful for parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Frozen RAFs are typically paired with a separate (higher) learning rate for the remaining network parameters.

Note on naming. RAF stands for Rational Activation Function, not “Rectified”; it is the learnable polynomial ratio described above.

Gated FFN Variants: SwiGLU, GEGLU, ReGLU

SwiGLU, GEGLU, and ReGLU  are gated feed-forward units that replace the standard \(\text{Linear}\to\text{activation}\to\text{Linear}\) block. They own their own linear projections and are therefore implemented as FFN modules, not as elementwise activations: \[\text{GatedFFN}(x) = \text{dropout}\!\Big(\, W_{\text{down}}\Big(\text{act}(x\,W_{\text{gate}}) \odot (x\,W_{\text{up}})\Big)\Big),\] where \(W_{\text{gate}}, W_{\text{up}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\text{ff}}}\) and \(W_{\text{down}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{ff}}\times d}\). The gate function is:

  • SwiGLU (swiglu): \(\text{act}=\text{SiLU}\) (the default, used in Llama, PaLM).

  • GEGLU (geglu): \(\text{act}=\text{GELU}\) (used in some T5 variants).

  • ReGLU (reglu): \(\text{act}=\text{ReLU}\) (cheapest option).

When ffn_activation is one of swiglu/geglu/reglu, the feed-forward layer swaps the standard dense and MoE FFN blocks for a gated FFN built with the same projection class (BitLinear under BitNet). Bias is disabled by default.

Configuration Schema

The ffn_activation_config object groups all learnable-activation parameters. It is optional and ignored for stateless activations.

  • raf_degrees: \([m,n]\) Padé numerator/denominator degrees (ints \(\ge 1\)). Default: \([5,4]\).

  • raf_version: denominator form, one of A (default), B, C, D, N.

  • raf_approx_func: initialization target. One of gelu (default), relu, leaky_relu, leaky_relu_, sigmoid, tanh, swish, silu, identity.

  • raf_trainable: freeze the rational parameters when false. Default: true.

  • raf_input_scaling: per-token min–max scaling to \([-3,3]\) before the rational (RAFT preprocessing). Default: false.

  • prelu_init: initial negative slope for PReLU. Default: \(0.25\).

  • elu_alpha: ELU saturation constant. Default: \(1.0\).

  • celu_alpha: CELU saturation constant. Default: \(1.0\).

  • swish_beta: fixed \(\beta\) for Swish / initial \(\beta\) for SwishTrainable. Default: \(1.0\).

  • leaky_relu_slope: negative slope for LeakyReLU. Default: \(0.01\).

  • maxout_pieces: number of linear pieces \(k\) for Maxout (int \(\ge 1\)). Default: \(2\).

  • Additional ELU-parametric keys: pelu_alpha, mpelu_alpha, mpelu_beta, felu_alpha, eelu_alpha, eelu_beta, pdelu_alpha, preu_alpha, preu_beta, softexp_alpha. All default to \(1.0\) (except softexp_alpha which defaults to \(0.0\)).

Selection Guide

The following decision tree aids activation choice:

  • Safe default \(\to\) silu (SiLU/Swish\(_1\), used in Llama, PaLM).

  • Classic stability \(\to\) gelu or relu.

  • Smooth non-monotonic \(\to\) mish or swish.

  • Mobile-friendly \(\to\) hardswish or relu6.

  • Learnable per-task shape \(\to\) raf, prelu, swish_trainable, or maxout.

  • Self-normalizing networks \(\to\) selu (with AlphaDropout).

  • Gated FFN (own projections) \(\to\) swiglu, geglu, or reglu.

With BitNet quantization, silu may be more robust than smooth activations that rely on precise gradient computation. Learnable activations (raf, prelu, swish_trainable) add parameters but can adapt to the task distribution.

Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC)

This annex documents the integration of Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) , a residual-connection framework that replaces the standard identity residual with an \(n\)-stream residual whose stream-mixing matrix is constrained to the Birkhoff polytope. The main body delegates to this annex for the mathematical formulation, the implementation details, and the reported results; the bibliography keys cited here resolve against .

Motivation: The Identity-Mapping Property

The standard residual connection propagates signals across depth unmodified: with \(x_l \in \mathbb{R}^{C}\) and a layer function \(F\), \[x_{l+1} = x_l + F(x_l, W_l),\] so that, recursively, \(x_L = x_l + \sum_{i=l}^{L-1} F(x_i, W_i)\). The direct term \(x_l\) (the identity mapping) lets information flow from shallow to deep layers unchanged, which He et al.  identified as key to stable training of very deep networks.

Hyper-Connections (HC) widen the residual stream by an expansion factor \(n\): the stream becomes \(x_l \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times C}\) while each layer’s internal function \(F\) still operates at dimension \(C\). Three learnable linear mappings govern the stream each layer:

  • \(H^{\text{pre}}_l \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}\) aggregates the \(nC\)-dimensional stream into the \(C\)-dimensional layer input;

  • \(H^{\text{post}}_l \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}\) maps the layer output back onto the stream;

  • \(H^{\text{res}}_l \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) mixes features within the residual stream.

The single-layer propagation is \[x_{l+1} = H^{\text{res}}_l x_l + \big(H^{\text{post}}_l\big)^{\!\top} F\big(H^{\text{pre}}_l x_l, W_l\big),\] and, recursively, the deep-to-shallow signal is governed by the composite mapping \(\prod_{i=L-1}^{l} H^{\text{res}}_{i+1}\). Because \(H^{\text{res}}_l\) is unconstrained in HC, this composite deviates from the identity, the stream norm is not conserved, and the forward/backward signal can be amplified or attenuated without bound. On a 27B-parameter MoE model the authors report composite gain magnitudes peaking near \(3000\) (versus \(1\) for the identity), correlating with gradient-norm spikes and an unexpected loss surge around step 12k. HC also multiplies memory-access cost by roughly \(n\) (the “memory wall”).

Formulation

Let \(x_l \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times C}\) be the stream at layer \(l\). The coefficients are computed from the flattened stream \(\tilde{x}_l = \operatorname{vec}(x_l) \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times nC}\): \[\tilde{H}_l = \frac{1}{r_l}\Big(\alpha \odot \big(\tilde{x}_l\, \varphi_l\big)\Big) + b_l, \qquad r_l = \frac{\|\tilde{x}_l\|_2}{\sqrt{nC}},\] where \(\varphi_l \in \mathbb{R}^{nC \times (n^2+2n)}\) is a learned linear projection, \(b_l \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times (n^2+2n)}\) a learned bias, and \(\alpha^{\text{pre}}, \alpha^{\text{post}}, \alpha^{\text{res}} \in \mathbb{R}\) are learnable gating scalars initialized to a small value (\(0.01\) in the paper and in this codebase). The scaling by \(1/r_l\) is mathematically equivalent to RMSNorm on the flattened stream, with the per-dimension scale absorbed into \(\varphi_l\). The three coefficient blocks are then: \[H^{\text{pre}}_l = \sigma\big(\tilde{H}^{\text{pre}}_l\big), \qquad H^{\text{post}}_l = 2\,\sigma\big(\tilde{H}^{\text{post}}_l\big), \qquad H^{\text{res}}_l = \mathrm{SK}\big(\exp(\tilde{H}^{\text{res}}_l)\big),\] where \(\sigma\) is the logistic sigmoid (enforcing non-negativity and preventing signal cancellation from mixed-sign coefficients) and \(\mathrm{SK}(\cdot)\) is the Sinkhorn–Knopp projection onto the set of doubly stochastic matrices \[\mathcal{M}^{\text{res}} = \big\{\, H \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} \;:\; H \ge 0,\;\; H\,\mathbf{1}_n = \mathbf{1}_n,\;\; \mathbf{1}_n^{\top} H = \mathbf{1}_n^{\top} \,\big\},\] i.e., the Birkhoff polytope (the convex hull of permutation matrices). Starting from \(M^{(0)} = \exp(\tilde{H}^{\text{res}}_l)\), the projection alternates row and column normalizations, \[M^{(t)} = T_c\big(T_r(M^{(t-1)})\big),\] for \(t = 1, \ldots, t_{\max}\) rounds (\(t_{\max} = 20\) by default in both the paper and this codebase). Finally the layer input and the updated stream are \[F^{\text{pre}}_l = H^{\text{pre}}_l x_l \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times C}, \qquad x_{l+1} = H^{\text{res}}_l x_l + \big(H^{\text{post}}_l\big)^{\!\top} \otimes F\big(F^{\text{pre}}_l, W_l\big).\]

Properties of the Manifold Constraint

Constraining \(H^{\text{res}}_l\) to the Birkhoff polytope restores the conservation behavior of the identity residual and guarantees three properties :

  1. Norm preservation: the spectral norm satisfies \(\|H^{\text{res}}_l\|_2 \le 1\) (non-expansive map), mitigating gradient explosion.

  2. Compositional closure: doubly stochastic matrices are closed under multiplication, so the composite \(\prod_i H^{\text{res}}_{i}\) remains doubly stochastic at arbitrary depth, preserving the identity-mapping property between any two depths.

  3. Geometric interpretation: since the Birkhoff polytope is the convex hull of permutation matrices, \(H^{\text{res}}_l x\) is a convex combination of feature permutations, i.e., a monotonic information-mixing mechanism across streams.

When \(n = 1\) the doubly stochastic condition degenerates to the scalar \(1\), recovering the exact identity mapping. With finite \(t_{\max}\) the projection is approximate, and the composite backward gain deviates from \(1\) but stays bounded (around \(1.6\) in the paper’s 27B runs, a \(\sim3\)-orders-of-magnitude reduction versus HC’s \(\approx 3000\)).

Implementation in Frankenstein Transformer

mHC is an opt-in replacement for the standard residual connection, controlled by the model.mhc sub-object (hierarchical schema) or the flat use_mhc keys, with additionalProperties: false at the sub-object level:

  • enabled (use_mhc, bool, default false): replace the standard residual with the n-stream residual.

  • expansion_rate (mhc_expansion_rate, int \(\ge 1\), default \(4\)): stream expansion factor \(n\); the stream becomes \(n \times \texttt{hidden\_\allowbreak size}\) while layer internals stay at hidden_size. \(1\) recovers the identity mapping.

  • sinkhorn_iters (mhc_sinkhorn_iters, int \(\ge 1\), default \(20\)): Sinkhorn–Knopp normalization rounds \(t_{\max}\).

  • gating_init (mhc_gating_init, float \(> 0\), default \(0.01\)): initial value of the gating scalars \(\alpha\).

  • checkpoint (mhc_checkpoint, bool, default false): gradient checkpointing on mHC layers, trading compute for memory to mitigate the \(\sim n{\times}\) activation-memory increase of the n-stream residual.

  • full_prec_under_bitnet (mhc_full_prec_under_bitnet, bool, default true): keep the coefficient projection \(\varphi_l\) a full-precision nn.Linear even when use_bitnet is true, avoiding ternary-quantization noise on the small mHC coefficients; when false (and BitNet enabled), \(\varphi_l\) uses BitLinear.

The module lives in :

  • SinkhornKnoppFunction (torch.autograd.Function): the forward pass applies the alternating row/column normalizations of \(\exp(\cdot)\); the backward pass recomputes the full iteration under torch.enable_grad and differentiates through it, obtaining the exact Jacobian-vector product (the recompute-on-chip strategy described in the paper).

  • ManifoldHyperConnections (nn.Module): holds \(\varphi_l\) (proj), \(b_l\) (bias) and the three gating scalars alpha_pre, alpha_post, alpha_res; exposes fpre (project the stream down to a layer input), recombine (update the stream with a layer output) and mappings (compute \(H^{\text{pre}}, H^{\text{post}}, H^{\text{res}}\)).

Wiring in :

  • HybridLayer gains optional mhc_attn and mhc_ffn modules (one mHC module per layer function); the _forward_dense_mhc path runs attention and FFN as layer functions over the shared \((B, S, n, C)\) stream.

  • FrankensteinTransformer expands the \(C\)-dimensional embedding to \((B, S, n, C)\) on entry via mhc_in_proj and collapses back to \(C\) via mhc_out_proj before the head.

  • mHC parameters route into the other optimizer parameter group.

  • mHC is incompatible with use_mixture_of_depths: MoD token routing operates on a single \(C\)-dimensional stream, conflicting with the n-stream residual; a ValueError is raised if both are enabled.

Example configuration: .

Reported Results

The paper evaluates mHC (and HC) with \(n = 4\), \(t_{\max} = 20\) and \(\alpha\)-init \(0.01\) on DeepSeek-V3-style MoE models (MLA attention, RoPE, RMSNorm, Loss-Free load balancing) from 3B to 27B parameters :

  • Stability: mHC removes HC’s loss surges (e.g., near step 12k on the 27B model) and keeps the composite residual gain bounded (\(\approx 1.6\) versus HC peaks \(\approx 3000\)).

  • Quality: on the 27B model mHC improves final training loss by \(0.021\) over the baseline, beats the baseline on all 8 downstream benchmarks (BBH, DROP, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MATH, MMLU, PIQA, TriviaQA) and HC on 7 of 8, with the largest gains on reasoning tasks (\(+2.1\) BBH, \(+2.3\) DROP over HC).

  • Scaling: the relative loss improvement over baseline is maintained across compute scales (3B \(\to\) 9B \(\to\) 27B) and across 1T tokens of token scaling.

  • Overhead: with fused kernels (TileLang), mixed-precision coefficient computation, selective recomputation, and DualPipe communication overlap, mHC adds only \(6.7\%\) additional training time at \(n = 4\) on the 27B model.

Hyperloop: Loop-Level Hyper-Connections on Looped Transformers

The Hyperloop Transformer combines looped Transformers — which reuse layer weights across depth — with loop-level hyper-connections, targeting parameter efficiency rather than raw depth. The layer stack is partitioned middle-cycle into a begin block (run once), a looped middle block, and an end block (run once); the looped middle block is wrapped in hyper-connections applied only after each loop iteration. With \(Y^{(l)}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times C}\) the matrix-valued stream at loop \(l\), \(z^{(l)}_t = \mathrm{RMSNorm}(\mathrm{flatten}(Y^{(l)}_t))\), and per-loop parameters \(\{W^{\tau}_l, b^{\tau}_l, \alpha^{\tau}_l\}\) for \(\tau \in \{\text{pre}, \text{post}, \text{res}\}\) plus a loop position embedding \(e_l \in \mathbb{R}^C\), the recurrence is \[y^{(l+1)}_t = H^{\text{res}}_l\, y^{(l)}_t + H^{\text{post}}_l \otimes \bigl( F(H^{\text{pre}}_l\, y^{(l)}_t) + e_l \bigr),\] with the data-dependent coefficients \[\begin{aligned} H^{\text{pre}}_l &= \sigma\bigl(\alpha^{\text{pre}}_l (W^{\text{pre}}_l z^{(l)}_t) + b^{\text{pre}}_l\bigr), & H^{\text{post}}_l &= 2\sigma\bigl(\alpha^{\text{post}}_l (W^{\text{post}}_l z^{(l)}_t) + b^{\text{post}}_l\bigr),\\ H^{\text{res}}_l &= \mathrm{diag}\bigl(\sigma(\alpha^{\text{res}}_l (W^{\text{res}}_l z^{(l)}_t) + b^{\text{res}}_l)\bigr) & W^{\text{res}}_l &\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times nC} \end{aligned}\] (the diagonal \(H^{\text{res}}\) substitutes mHC’s \(\mathrm{sinkhorn}(\cdot)\) over a dense \(n^2 \times nC\) projection with a sigmoid over a diagonal gate — the paper’s Table 6 ablation finds this both cheaper and more accurate: 14.40 perplexity versus 14.59 Sinkhorn and 14.61 identity).

Four properties distinguish the Hyperloop wiring from per-sublayer mHC (§22): (1) hyper-connections fire once per loop, not after every sub-layer — also the most performant placement in the paper’s Table 5 ablation; (2) the stream is created by copying the begin-block output \(n\) times and collapsed by averaging the streams before the end block, replacing mHC’s learned in/out projections; (3) the parameters are per loop, relaxing the strict weight sharing of ordinary looped Transformers — the paper’s representation-similarity analysis (Table 8) shows looped-layer representations deviate more across loops, which it identifies as the source of the quality gains; and (4) \(H^{\text{res}}\) defaults to the diagonal-sigmoid parameterization.

The Frankenstein integration is controlled by the mhc.hyperloop boolean (flat mhc_hyperloop; requires mhc.enabled and dims.num_loops \(\ge 2\)), with three additional keys:

  • hyperloop_begin_layers / hyperloop_end_layers (int \(\ge 0\), default \(0\)): sizes of the begin/end blocks, which run exactly once. The paper allocates \(\sim\)25% of parameters to each and 50% to the middle block (unrolled depth \(=\) begin \(+\) middle \(\times\) loops \(+\) end; e.g. \(2L \to 4L(\times3) \to 2L\) at 16 layers). \(0/0\) loops the whole stack.

  • hyperloop_res_parameterization (enum, default diagonal): diagonal, sinkhorn (full mHC-style doubly stochastic mixing, reusing SinkhornKnoppFunction) or identity.

Implementation: hosts HyperloopConnections with per-loop projs / biases / alphas_ / loop_pos_embs (\(e_l\), zero-initialized so that at initialisation the update reduces to the plain looped-Transformer recurrence). FrankensteinEncoder (and FrankensteinViT) build it instead of the mhc_in_proj/mhc_out_proj pair; the forward pass runs begin \(\to\) copy \(\to\) per-loop read/middle/update \(\to\) average \(\to\) end. HybridLayer disables its per-layer mhc_attn/mhc_ffn modules under Hyperloop, so middle-block layers run the standard \(C\)-dimensional path — which restores Mixture-of-Depths compatibility (per-layer mHC forbids MoD). Hyperloop is incompatible with the AttnRes residuals (residuals.type full_attn / block_attn), which assume a per-logical-layer n-stream residual. The per-loop parameter budget is \(3n^2C + 3n + 3 + C\) (diagonal): for the paper’s 136M model (\(C = 1024\), \(n = 4\), 3 loops) only \(\approx\)150K parameters beyond the plain looped Transformer.

Example configuration: .

Reported results (arXiv:2604.21254)

Trained on FineWeb-Edu with \(n = 4\) streams and 3 loops (25%/50%/25% parameter split), against depth-matched Transformer and mHC baselines:

  • Parameter efficiency: at 240M/1B/2B depth-matched scale, Hyperloop uses \(\approx\)50% fewer parameters (136M/580M/991M) yet matches or beats the baselines in perplexity (14.40 vs 14.65 at 240M scale; 9.65 vs 10.19 at 1B; 8.49 vs 8.60 at 2B).

  • Quantization: INT4 (GPTQ) perplexity degrades less than the vanilla looped model (14.68 vs 15.18 at 240M scale), so the parameter savings survive post-training compression.

  • Overhead: loop-level placement plus the diagonal \(H^{\text{res}}\) keep the training throughput within \(\approx\)5% of the plain looped Transformer in unoptimized PyTorch (per-layer mHC loses \(\approx\)33% without fused kernels).

  • Ablations: every-loop placement beats every-layer (Table 5); diagonal \(H^{\text{res}}\) beats Sinkhorn and identity (Table 6); stream count \(n\) shows diminishing returns beyond 4 (Table 4); LoRA-per-loop (relaxed recursive Transformers) helps far less per parameter than the hyper-connection relaxation (Table 7).

Attention Residuals (AttnRes)

This annex documents the integration of Attention Residuals (AttnRes) , a generalization of the residual connection that replaces the fixed unit-coefficient residual sum with learned softmax attention over depth. The main body delegates to this annex for the mathematical formulation, the four available strategies (standard, no-residual, Full AttnRes, Block AttnRes), the implementation wiring, the integration with mHC and Mixture-of-Depths, and the reported results. The bibliography keys cited here resolve against .

Motivation: From a Fixed Sum to Depth-Wise Attention

The standard residual connection propagates signals across depth unmodified: with \(x_l \in \mathbb{R}^{C}\) and a layer function \(F\), \[x_{l+1} = x_l + F(x_l, W_l),\] so that, recursively, \(x_L = x_l + \sum_{i=l}^{L-1} F(x_i, W_i)\). The identity term \(x_l\) (the identity mapping) lets information flow from shallow to deep layers unchanged, which He et al.  identified as key to stable training of very deep networks. Highway networks generalize this with learned element-wise gates \(\mathbf{g}_l \in [0, 1]^{C}\), \[x_{l+1} = (1 - \mathbf{g}_l) \odot x_l + \mathbf{g}_l \odot F(x_l, W_l),\] which interpolates between the identity path and the transformation path with input-dependent weights.

Attention Residuals take the next step: instead of weighting a single compressed state \(x_l\), layer \(l\) attends over all earlier layer outputs. Let \(v_0 = h_1\) (the token embedding) and \(v_i = F(x_i, W_i)\) for \(i \ge 1\). AttnRes computes, for each layer \(l\), \[q_l = w_l, \qquad k_i = \mathrm{RMSNorm}(v_i), \qquad \alpha_{i \to l} = \mathrm{softmax}_i(q_l^{\top} k_i), \qquad x_{l+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{l} \alpha_{i \to l} \, v_i,\] where \(w_l \in \mathbb{R}^{C}\) is a learned per-layer pseudo-query, initialized to zero per the paper. At zero-init the softmax is uniform, so AttnRes degenerates to an equal-weight average of all previous outputs — matching the standard residual at step zero and avoiding training volatility. The RMSNorm on the keys prevents layers with naturally large magnitudes from dominating the softmax (ablation in the paper: § 5.3).

Four Strategies

The schema field model.residuals.type selects one of four strategies, each implemented as a separate module under .

Standard Residual ("standard")

The default backwards-compatible strategy: \[x_{l+1} = x_l + F(x_l, W_l).\] Stateless, no extra parameters, no extra compute. Implemented as a no-op pass-through in StandardResidual that delegates the merge to HybridLayer.

No Residual ("none", experimental)

Drops the skip connection entirely: \[x_{l+1} = F(x_l, W_l).\] Stateless, no extra parameters. Useful only as an ablation probe; the identity term is critical for deep stacks (paper § 2.1) and training is typically unstable without it. Implemented as NoResidual.

Full Attention Residuals ("full_attn", paper § 3.1)

Each layer attends over all previous layer outputs: \[x_{l+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{l} \alpha_{i \to l} \, v_i, \qquad \alpha_{i \to l} = \mathrm{softmax}_i\!\big(w_l^{\top} \mathrm{RMSNorm}(v_i)\big).\] Adds \(L \cdot C\) parameters (\(L\) = logical depth = num_layers \(\times\) num_loops, \(C\) = hidden_size), one query vector per layer. Memory and compute grow as \(O(L \, d)\) per token; at typical depth (\(L < 1000\)) this is negligible. Implemented as FullAttentionResidual; supports attnres_gradient_checkpoint to wrap the attention in torch.utils.checkpoint for memory-constrained runs.

Block Attention Residuals ("block_attn", paper § 3.2)

Partitions the \(L\) logical layers into \(N\) blocks of \(S = \lceil L / N \rceil\) layers each. Within a block the layer outputs accumulate as a standard partial sum \(b_n^i\); across blocks attention is applied over the \(N\) complete block representations and the running partial sum. For layer \(l\) in block \(n\), \[x_{l+1} = \sum_{m=0}^{n} \alpha_{m \to l} \, v_m, \qquad \alpha_{m \to l} = \mathrm{softmax}_m\!\big(w_l^{\top} \mathrm{RMSNorm}(v_m)\big),\] with \(v_m = b_m\) for \(m < n\) and \(v_n = b_n^{i_l}\) (the current intra-block partial sum). \(N\) interpolates between Full AttnRes (\(N = L\), one block per layer) and standard residuals (\(N = 1\), the embedding isolated as \(b_0\)). The paper’s empirical sweet spot is \(N \approx 8\); this codebase defaults to \(N = 8\) and validates that \(N \le L\). Implemented as BlockAttentionResidual, which also follows Algorithm 1 of the paper (two-phase computation with online softmax merging).

Implementation in Frankenstein Transformer

The package hosts one class per strategy (StandardResidual, NoResidual, FullAttentionResidual, BlockAttentionResidual) plus an abstract ResidualBase that defines the lifecycle hooks set_streams, register_state, reset_state, forward, and finalize. The build_residual(config) factory in selects the right class from FrankensteinModelConfig.

Wiring in :

  • FrankensteinEncoder owns the ResidualBase module as self.residual; the factory is invoked once in __init__.

  • Before the looped-depth loop the encoder calls reset_state and, for AttnRes variants, set_embedding(x) so the depth-wise attention knows the \(v_0 = h_1\) source.

  • After each HybridLayer call, if self.residual.is_attn_res is true, the encoder applies x = self.residual(layer_idx, x) to overwrite the stream with the attended aggregation. For stateless strategies (standard, none) this step is skipped and HybridLayer continues to apply its own residual merge internally.

Wiring in :

  • HybridLayer reads residual_type from the config and dispatches the residual merge accordingly. For standard the merge is the original x = residual + mixer(norm(x)); for none the skip is dropped (x = mixer(norm(x))); for the AttnRes variants the layer performs the standard merge internally because the depth-wise attention is applied externally by the encoder.

  • _forward_dense_mhc (the mHC path) is unaffected because mHC has its own stream-expansion residual; combining AttnRes with mHC is handled by the mhc_stream_mode field of the residual module.

Schema (hierarchical, with the flat-key renames shown in parentheses) and defaults:

  • model.residuals.type (residual_type, enum [standard, none, full_attn, block_attn], default standard): selects the strategy.

  • model.residuals.full_attn.init_query_zero (full_attn_init_query_zero, bool, default true): zero-init the per-layer query vectors \(\mathbf{w}_l\).

  • model.residuals.full_attn.use_rmsnorm_keys (full_attn_use_rmsnorm_keys, bool, default true): apply RMSNorm on keys before the dot product.

  • model.residuals.block_attn.num_blocks (block_attn_num_blocks, int \(\ge 1\), default \(8\)): number of block representations \(N\); validated \(N \le L\).

  • model.residuals.block_attn.init_query_zero (block_attn_init_query_zero, bool, default true): zero-init the per-layer query vectors.

  • model.residuals.block_attn.use_rmsnorm_keys (block_attn_use_rmsnorm_keys, bool, default true): RMSNorm on keys.

  • model.residuals.mhc_stream_mode (attnres_mhc_stream_mode, enum [independent, joint], default independent): how AttnRes interacts with mHC’s n-stream residual.

  • model.residuals.gradient_checkpoint (attnres_gradient_checkpoint, bool, default false): wrap the AttnRes attention in gradient checkpointing.

Integration with mHC and Mixture-of-Depths

The residual strategy is orthogonal to mHC and Mixture-of-Depths (MoD): all combinations are supported. The interaction modes are:

mHC \(\times\) AttnRes (mhc_stream_mode).

When use_mhc=true and the residual is full_attn or block_attn, the depth-wise attention is applied either per stream ("independent") or over the flattened \(nC\)-dim projection ("joint"). Independent mode runs \(n\) parallel attentions, one per stream — matching the paper’s framing where each stream is a parallel "view" of the residual. Joint mode treats the \(n\) streams as a single fat residual, more expressive but more parameter-hungry. The mHC coefficient projections (\(\varphi_l\), \(b_l\), \(\alpha\) gates) are unaffected; AttnRes adds its own parameters on top.

Mixture-of-Depths \(\times\) AttnRes.

MoD token routing operates within a layer (selects which tokens get the full layer update) and is orthogonal to the residual choice. When use_mixture_of_depths=true together with an AttnRes residual, only the tokens selected by MoD contribute to the layer-output buffer (Full AttnRes) or the intra-block partial sum (Block AttnRes); the rest pass through unchanged and are scattered back by MoD’s existing logic. MoD is mutually exclusive with mHC (a ValueError is raised in HybridLayer._init__ if both are enabled); the corresponding combinations are \((\text{no\_\allowbreak mHC}, \text{MoD}, \text{AttnRes})\), \((\text{mHC}, \text{no\_\allowbreak MoD}, \text{AttnRes})\), or \((\text{mHC}, \text{no\_\allowbreak MoD}, \text{no\_\allowbreak AttnRes})\).

Reported Results

The paper validates AttnRes through scaling laws, ablations, and a 48B-parameter Kimi Linear extension:

  • Scaling laws: both Full and Block AttnRes consistently outperform the PreNorm baseline across five model sizes. At 5.6 PFLOP/s-days, Block AttnRes reaches loss \(1.692\) versus the baseline’s \(1.714\) — equivalent to a \(1.25 \times\) compute advantage. The gap between Full and Block AttnRes narrows with scale (Full \(1.737\) vs. Block \(1.746\) on the 16-layer model).

  • Ablations: input-dependent softmax attention (\(1.737\)) outperforms input-independent scalar mixing (\(1.749\)) and sigmoid attention (\(1.741\)). RMSNorm on keys is essential (Full \(1.737\) vs. \(1.743\) without; Block \(1.746\) vs. \(1.750\)). Multi-head depth aggregation (\(\texttt{H} = 16\)) hurts Block AttnRes (\(1.752\) vs. \(1.746\)), indicating the optimal mixture is largely uniform across channels. Sliding-window attention over the last \(W = 8\) layers falls short of Block AttnRes (\(1.764\) vs. \(1.746\)).

  • Kimi Linear extension: a 48B-parameter (3B activated) Kimi Linear model with Block AttnRes (\(N \approx 9\), \(S = 6\)) pre-trained on 1.4T tokens improves over the baseline across all 14 downstream benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond, BBH, HellaSwag, TriviaQA, GSM8K, MGSM, Math, CMath, HumanEval, MBPP, CMMLU, C-Eval, ARC-C). The largest gains are on multi-step reasoning (GPQA-Diamond \(+7.5\), Minerva Math \(+3.6\)) and code generation (HumanEval \(+3.1\)). Training-dynamics analysis shows that AttnRes mitigates PreNorm dilution: hidden-state magnitudes remain bounded across depth and gradient norms distribute more uniformly across layers.

  • Overhead: training overhead is marginal when pipeline parallelism is not enabled; with pipeline parallelism Block AttnRes adds \(<4\%\) end-to-end training overhead (cross-stage caching eliminates redundant transfers) and \(<2\%\) inference latency overhead (two-phase computation with online softmax merging).
