Relation to Prior Work

  • KV-cache quantization (KIVI, KVQuant, SKVQ): adopted as write-time codecs with asymmetric granularity and protected outlier regions; the group-window append semantics follow KIVI’s residual window.

  • Eviction and sparsity (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV, Quest): adopted as read-time policies; Quest-style page metadata and query-aware reading are future work inside the slot extras.

  • Paged and prefix sharing (PagedAttention/vLLM, RadixAttention): structurally compatible — slots are content-agnostic and serializable — but block tables and prefix sharing are out of scope for v1.

  • Hybrid schedulers (Jamba, Griffin, Zamba): the same slot dictionary holds attention K/V and recurrent states, which is the pattern these systems established.

  • Speculative decoding and early exit (LayerSkip): served by the same truncate primitive that the tests exercise.

When to enable the cache.

Any decoder-only generation workload benefits: the regime where decode dominates (long outputs, short prompts) gains the most, while a single full forward (classification, embedding, masked prediction) gains nothing and should leave enabled false. Quantization is worth enabling when memory, not latency, is the binding constraint, and int4_kivi should keep a protected window of at least the attention-sink span; window-with-sinks eviction is the right default for streaming or unbounded contexts. For recurrent layers the state is already constant-size, so eviction is meaningless and quantization is disabled by design.

Numerically Fixed Softmax and Cross-Entropy

Standard implementations of softmax, log-softmax and cross-entropy subtract the maximum logit before exponentiating, which prevents overflow but leaves two floating-point defects . The first, Softmax Collapse, rounds the target (or argmax) gradient to zero once the logits become sufficiently confident, breaking the zero-sum property of the gradient and producing the “Slingshot” loss spikes observed with adaptive optimizers. The second, Softmax Cancellation, degrades soft-target (distillation) gradients when student and teacher logits nearly coincide. This annex documents the toolkit’s opt-in implementation of the first fix — cancellation-free softmax, log-softmax and hard-target cross-entropy — its custom backward pass, its integration surface and its validation. Soft-target cross-entropy is out of scope because the toolkit exposes no distillation objective; the sentence-embedding path delegates its losses to sentence-transformers.

The Two Floating-Point Defects

For logits \(z \in \mathbb{R}^{K}\) and target class \(t\), the standard stabilised computations are \[\tilde{z}_k = z_k - z_{\max}, \qquad \operatorname{logsoftmax}(z)_k = \tilde{z}_k - \log \sum_j e^{\tilde{z}_j}, \qquad q_k = \frac{e^{\tilde{z}_k}}{\sum_j e^{\tilde{z}_j}}, \label{eq:standard-softmax}\] and the cross-entropy is \(L(z,t) = -\operatorname{logsoftmax}(z)_t\), whose exact gradient is \(g = q - p\) for a target distribution \(p\).

Softmax Collapse.

Define the logit margin \[m = z_t - \log \sum_{j \neq t} e^{z_j}. \label{eq:margin}\] When the target is also the maximum logit, \(\tilde{z}_t = 0\) and the denominator becomes \(1 + e^{-m}\). Floating-point numbers are much denser near zero than near one: in fp32, values near \(0\) resolve down to \(\sim\!10^{-38}\), while terms added to \(1.0\) are lost below the unit roundoff \(u = 2^{-p}\). The denominator therefore rounds to exactly \(1.0\) once \(m\) exceeds the precision cliff \[c_d = -\ln u = p \ln 2 , \qquad c_{16} \approx 5.5, \quad c_{32} \approx 16.6, \quad c_{64} \approx 36.7, \label{eq:cliff}\] for bf16 (\(p = 8\)), fp32 (\(p = 24\)) and fp64 (\(p = 53\)). Past the cliff, the forward loss becomes \(\log(1) = 0\) and the target gradient \(q_t - 1\) becomes exactly \(0\), while the non-target gradients \(q_j = e^{z_j - z_t}/(1 + e^{-m})\) remain positive down to exponent underflow (\(m \approx 88\) in fp32). The gradient no longer sums to zero, \[\sum_k g_k \approx \sum_{j \neq t} q_j > 0 , \label{eq:broken-zero-sum}\] which biases every parameter update and interacts badly with Adam’s per-coordinate normalisation: when the missing target gradient later reappears, the second-moment estimate has decayed and the update spikes.

Softmax Cancellation.

For soft targets \(p = \operatorname{softmax}(z^{T})\), the gradient \(q - p\) is the difference of two nearly equal probability vectors. Computing them separately loses the small difference that carries the signal and leaves a non-zero residual even when \(z^{S} = z^{T}\). The paper’s fix computes the difference directly in log space with expm1/log1p; this toolkit has no distillation loss and therefore does not implement it.

Cancellation-Free Formulations

Both fixes exclude the argmax entry from the log-sum-exp and reintroduce it through a stable softplus. Let \(a = \arg\max_k z_k\), \(z_{\max} = z_a\), and \[s = \operatorname{softplus}\!\left(-m\right) = \log\!\left(1 + e^{-m}\right) = \log \sum_{j \neq a} e^{z_j - z_{\max}} , \qquad m = z_{\max} - \log \sum_{j \neq a} e^{z_j}. \label{eq:softplus-margin}\] Then \[\operatorname{logsoftmax}(z)_k = z_k - z_{\max} - s, \qquad q_k = \exp\!\left(z_k - z_{\max} - s\right), \label{eq:fixed-values}\] with the argmax entry evaluated as exactly \(-s\) and \(\exp(-s)\) respectively. Because \(s\) is computed as \(\log(1 + e^{-m})\) (equivalently \(\log\!\operatorname{1p}(e^{-m})\)), the tiny \(e^{-m}\) term survives far beyond the standard cliff, down to exponent underflow.

The complement of the maximum probability is the load-bearing quantity for the backward pass. Rather than forming \(1 - q_{\max}\) (which cancels in the output dtype), the implementation uses the identity \[1 - q_{\max} = -\operatorname{expm1}(-s), \label{eq:one-minus-qmax}\] which is accurate for arbitrarily small \(s\).

Hard-target cross-entropy.

Using the target logit as the reference, the loss is \[L(z,t) = \operatorname{softplus}\!\left(\operatorname{logsumexp}_{j \neq t}\left(z_j - z_t\right)\right) = \log\!\left(1 + \sum_{j \neq t} e^{z_j - z_t}\right), \label{eq:fixed-ce}\] which is algebraically identical to \(\log(1 + e^{-m})\) but never adds the small term to one. Writing \(z_t\) through the differences \(z_j - z_t\) makes automatic differentiation return \[g_t = -\frac{e^{-m}}{1 + e^{-m}}, \qquad g_j = \frac{e^{z_j - z_t}}{1 + e^{-m}} \quad (j \neq t), \label{eq:fixed-gradients}\] so the target gradient is obtained as minus the sum of the non-target gradients and \(\sum_k g_k = 0\) holds by construction, at any margin. The magnitude \(e^{-m}/(1+e^{-m})\) is preserved down to exponent underflow — precisely the component the standard implementation rounds to zero.

Softmax and log-softmax Jacobians.

For a standalone softmax the forward values of Equation [eq:fixed-values] may still round to one in the output dtype (that is unavoidable for the stored probability), but the Jacobian must not collapse. Given an upstream gradient \(g\), the softmax vector–Jacobian product is \[\frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = q \odot \left(g - \langle g, q\rangle\right), \label{eq:softmax-vjp}\] whose argmax entry is rewritten as \[\left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_a}\right|_{\text{fixed}} = q_{\max}\left(g_{\max}\,(1 - q_{\max}) - \sum_{j \neq a} g_j q_j\right), \label{eq:argmax-vjp}\] with \(1 - q_{\max}\) taken from Equation [eq:one-minus-qmax]. The true Jacobian entry \(q_{\max}(1 - q_{\max}) \approx e^{-m}\) thus survives the cliff. For log-softmax (\(\partial \operatorname{logsoftmax}_k/\partial z_j = \delta_{kj} - q_j\)) the argmax entry is likewise rewritten as \[\left.\frac{\partial L}{\partial z_a}\right|_{\text{fixed}} = -\sum_{j \neq a} g_j + (1 - q_{\max}) \sum_k g_k . \label{eq:logsoftmax-vjp}\]

Table [tab:collapse-regimes] contrasts the two regimes. The values are the exact quantities of Equations [eq:fixed-gradients]–[eq:argmax-vjp]; the standard column is what Equation [eq:standard-softmax] produces once \(m > c_d\).

L3.9cmL4.5cmL4.5cm Quantity & Standard & Fixed
\(q_{\max}\) & \(1.0\) (rounded) & \(e^{-s}\) (values; may round)
\(1 - q_{\max}\) & \(0.0\) (rounded) & \(-\operatorname{expm1}(-s)\)
CE loss & \(\log(1)=0\) & \(\operatorname{softplus}(s)>0\)
\(g_t\) & \(0.0\) & \(-e^{-m}/(1+e^{-m})\)
\(\sum_k g_k\) & \(\sum_{j \neq t} q_j > 0\) & \(0\) (by construction)
\(\partial q_{\max}/\partial z_{\max}\) & \(0.0\) & \(q_{\max}(1-q_{\max})\)

Implementation in the Toolkit

The fixes live in and are exposed as two boolean checkboxes under the model.numerics schema group, both defaulting to false:

model:
  numerics:
    fixed_softmax: true          # every explicit softmax / log-softmax
    fixed_cross_entropy: true    # hard-target task losses

Neither flag adds parameters, buffers or state-dict entries, so checkpoints, parameter counting and export (PyTorch, Transformers, GGUF) are unaffected; the flags travel with the model configuration. When disabled, the code paths reduce to the original torch calls with a single attribute lookup per softmax, so the default behaviour and performance are unchanged. The fixed losses accept the same ignore_index and reduction semantics as torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy and compute in the input dtype (no implicit upcast), which keeps the fix effective in bf16 as well as fp32/fp64.

Backward Pass

PyTorch’s autograd graph for Equation [eq:fixed-values] still contains the subtraction that produces \(1 - q_{\max}\), and evaluating it there re-introduces the cancellation. The implementation therefore defines the two softmax functions as torch.autograd.Function objects whose forward computes Equation [eq:fixed-values] and whose backward uses Equations [eq:softmax-vjp]–[eq:logsoftmax-vjp]. The cross-entropy needs no custom backward: the graph of Equation [eq:fixed-ce] already yields Equation [eq:fixed-gradients] exactly, because \(z_t\) enters every shifted logit with coefficient \(-1\) and the target row is excluded from the log-sum-exp.

logits \(z \in \mathbb{R}^{K}\) along a normalisation axis, upstream gradient \(g\) \(a \gets \arg\max_k z_k\), \(z_{\max} \gets z_a\) \(\ell \gets \operatorname{logsumexp}\{z_k - z_{\max} : k \neq a\}\) \(s \gets \operatorname{softplus}(\ell)\) \(c \gets -\operatorname{expm1}(-s)\) \(q \gets \exp(z - z_{\max} - s)\) backward: \(\tau \gets \sum_k g_k q_k\), \(\sigma \gets \sum_{k \neq a} g_k q_k\) \(\nabla z \gets q \odot (g - \tau)\) \(\nabla z_a \gets q_a\left(g_a\,c - \sigma\right)\) return \(q\); return \(\nabla z\)

Integration Surface

A single switch must reach every place where the toolkit materialises probabilities or logits. HybridLayer attaches the resolved flag to each mixer as use_fixed_softmax; the residual factory does the same for the depth-wise attention residuals; the KV-cache hooks take an explicit use_fixed_softmax argument. A dispatch helper then selects the implementation per call site. Table [tab:fixed-coverage] lists the covered surfaces.

L4.1cmL8.8cm Surface & Covered sites
Attention mixers & standard, titan, gqa, ode; latent family (mla, gqla, mlra, tucker, iha, gta, mtla, cca, ccgqa, gma); gated (gated_softmax, fox); sparse (fasa, sparge, msa, nsa, bigbird, longformer, sparse_transformer, sparsek, swa, sparda); dense surrogate of training-free mixers
Routers & MoE and Mixture-of-Depths top-\(k\) softmax
Residuals & Full and Block AttnRes depth-wise softmax
KV cache & recompute/fallback normaliser in src/model/cache/hooks.py
Decoding & top-\(p\) nucleus filtering and final sampling distribution
Deployment & inference.predict probability readout
Training losses & mlm, causal_lm, classification, segmentation (CE and Dice softmax), text_classification, patch_prediction

The loss side is dispatched by a single trainer helper, so every task shares the same semantics:

def _task_cross_entropy(self, logits, targets, **kwargs):
    if self._use_fixed_cross_entropy():
        return fixed_cross_entropy(
            logits, targets, ignore_index=kwargs.get("ignore_index", -100))
    return F.cross_entropy(logits, targets, **kwargs)

Cost, Scope and Validation

Cost.

The fixed paths have the same asymptotic complexity as the standard ones and touch each row with a constant number of extra element-wise operations (one masked log-sum-exp and one softplus; one expm1 in the backward). There are no matrix multiplications, no additional memory of order \(K\) beyond temporaries, and no parameters. On ordinary logits the fixed and standard values agree to within floating-point tolerance; only the sub-roundoff regime that the standard path collapses changes.

Scope.

The flags target hard-target classification-style losses. Soft-target cross-entropy (knowledge distillation, KL regularisation) would need the paper’s expm1/log1p difference construction, which this toolkit does not implement because it has no distillation path. The SSOG mixer’s internal LSE kernels, and the sigmoid attention normaliser (which is not a softmax), are intentionally left unchanged.

Validation.

The repository ships , which asserts (i) forward parity with torch for softmax, log-softmax and cross-entropy in fp32/fp64, including masked (\(-\infty\)) and single-key inputs; (ii) the cliff regressions of Table [tab:collapse-regimes] at margins \(25 > c_{32}\) and \(40 > c_{64}\) — the standard target/argmax gradients are exactly zero and the fixed ones are not, with a zero-sum gradient in the fixed case; (iii) ignore_index, reduction and dispatch semantics; (iv) full-model forward parity (fixed versus standard is mathematically identical) and finite backward passes; (v) KV-cache prefill\(+\)decode parity with the flag enabled; and (vi) trainer dispatch. The combinatoric end-to-end harness additionally trains real MLM and causal-LM models with fixed_softmax, fixed_cross_entropy, both together, and the interplay with SSMax and BitNet, all on CPU. A ready-to-run preset is .

When to enable.

The fix matters when logit margins can grow large during training: small algorithmic datasets that exhibit grokking, long training with weight decay and adaptive optimizers, and any regime where the loss becomes extremely confident. In ordinary large-scale training the standard path is usually indistinguishable; the fixed path is a safe default candidate because it is mathematically identical in the forward pass and strictly better conditioned in the backward pass.

Conformer: Convolution-Augmented Self-Attention

Executive Summary

The Conformer block is the toolkit’s convolution-augmented sequence mixer, exposed as conformer. It keeps the global receptive field of scaled dot-product attention and adds a depthwise-convolution branch that models local, narrow-band structure—the inductive bias speech recognition needs and the one plain self-attention lacks. The block sandwiches multi-head self-attention (MHSA) with relative sinusoidal positional encodings between two Macaron-style half-step feed-forward layers , and inserts the convolution module between the attention and the second FFN. In the reference recipe it reaches \(1.9\%\)/\(3.9\%\) WER on LibriSpeech test-clean/test-other without an external language model (Conformer-L, 118.8M parameters), and it is the mixer recommended for the audio model class of Appendix 31. The toolkit runs both feed-forward layers at full step (the paper’s “full-step” variant of its Table 5) and lets the outer layer own the second one; Table [tab:conformer-mapping] lists the deviations.

The mixer is available to every model class: the text encoder, the causal decoder (where depthwise padding is shifted to stay streaming-safe), the Vision Transformer, and frankenstein_audio. Because the block lives inside HybridLayer, it composes with all 45 mixers, the 6 norms, the 4 residual strategies, MoE, Mixture-of-Depths, mHC, AttnRes, BitNet and the 23 optimizer families.

Conformer: Convolution-augmented Attention

Mathematical Formulation

For a block input \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times d}\) the reference block of Fig. 1 of is \[\begin{aligned} \tilde{x} &= x + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{FFN}_1\big(\mathrm{LN}(x)\big), \label{eq:conformer-ffn1}\\ x' &= \tilde{x} + \mathrm{MHSA}\big(\mathrm{LN}(\tilde{x})\big), \label{eq:conformer-mhsa}\\ x'' &= x' + \mathrm{Conv}\big(\mathrm{LN}(x')\big), \label{eq:conformer-conv}\\ y &= \mathrm{LN}\Big(x'' + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{FFN}_2\big(x''\big)\Big). \label{eq:conformer-ffn2} \end{aligned}\] The two feed-forward terms carry the Macaron half-step coefficient: each contributes half of a full residual update, one before and one after the attention–convolution pair.

Feed-forward module.

With hidden width \(d_{ff}\), \[\mathrm{FFN}(x) = W_2\,\mathrm{Dropout}\big(\mathrm{Swish}(W_1\,\mathrm{LN}(x) + b_1)\big) + b_2, \qquad \mathrm{Swish}(a) = a\,\sigma(a), \label{eq:conformer-ffn}\] where \(W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{ff} \times d}\), \(W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_{ff}}\) and \(\sigma\) is the logistic sigmoid. The paper uses \(d_{ff} = 4d\).

Multi-head self-attention with relative positional encoding.

Queries, keys and values are linear projections of the normalized block input, \(Q = \mathrm{LN}(\tilde{x})W_Q\), \(K = \mathrm{LN}(\tilde{x})W_K\), \(V = \mathrm{LN}(\tilde{x})W_V\), split into \(H\) heads of width \(d_h = d/H\). Following the Transformer-XL relative scheme , the score of query \(i\) against key \(j\) adds a sinusoidal function of the displacement \(i-j\) instead of an absolute position: \[e_{ij} = q_i^{\top} k_j + (q_i + v)^{\top} R_{i-j}, \qquad A_{ij} = \operatorname{softmax}_j\!\Big(\frac{e_{ij}}{\sqrt{d_h}}\Big), \qquad O = A V W_O, \label{eq:conformer-relpe}\] with \(v\) a learned bias vector and, for \(m = 0, \dots, d_h/2 - 1\), \[R_{\delta,\,2m} = \sin\!\big(\delta\,/\,10000^{2m/d_h}\big), \qquad R_{\delta,\,2m+1} = \cos\!\big(\delta\,/\,10000^{2m/d_h}\big). \label{eq:conformer-sinusoid}\] Because the encoding depends only on \(\delta = i-j\), the block generalizes across utterance lengths. The toolkit routes positional information through the model-wide machinery that every other mixer uses: model.positional_encoding (RoPE by default) is applied to \(Q/K\), and conformer_use_pe (default true) lets a layer opt out. The paper’s relative sinusoidal scheme is closest to sinusoidal_rotary (sinusoidal frequencies applied as a rotation on \(Q/K\), relative by construction); alibi/bam supply a distance bias instead of a rotation. A dedicated Transformer-XL-style relative-sinusoidal module is not implemented. In decoder mode the score matrix receives the usual causal mask before the softmax, and the fixed-softmax path of Appendix 29.3 is used when numerics.fixed_softmax is enabled.

Convolution module.

The module applies a gated depthwise convolution over the time axis: \[\begin{aligned} h &= \mathrm{LN}(x'), \\ [u,\, g] &= \mathrm{Conv1d}_{d \to 2d}(h), \qquad \tilde{h} = u \odot \sigma(g), \label{eq:conformer-glu}\\ z_t &= \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} w_k\, \tilde{h}_{t + k - \lfloor K/2 \rfloor}, \label{eq:conformer-depthwise}\\ c &= \mathrm{Dropout}\Big(\mathrm{Conv1d}_{d \to d}\big(\mathrm{Swish}(\mathrm{BN}(z))\big)\Big), \label{eq:conformer-conv-out} \end{aligned}\] where \(\odot\) is the elementwise product (a GLU that halves the \(2d\) channels back to \(d\)), \(w \in \mathbb{R}^{K}\) is the depthwise kernel and \(\mathrm{BN}\) normalizes each channel over the batch and time axes, \[\mathrm{BN}(z)_{b,t,c} = \gamma_c\,\frac{z_{b,t,c} - \mu_c}{\sqrt{\sigma_c^2 + \epsilon}} + \beta_c . \label{eq:conformer-bn}\] In decoder mode the sum in Equation [eq:conformer-depthwise] is shifted to \(z_t = \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} w_k \tilde{h}_{t-K+1+k}\), so that no future frame enters the convolution; encoder and ViT modes keep the symmetric “same” padding of the paper.

Algorithmic Pseudocode

block input \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times d}\), kernel \(K=32\), heads \(H\), Macaron flag, mode block-level delta \(\Delta\) such that \(x + \Delta\) enters the outer \(\mathrm{norm}_2 + \mathrm{FFN}_2\) \(\tilde{x} \gets x + \mathrm{FFN}_1(\mathrm{LN}(x))\) \(Q, K_{proj}, V \gets \mathrm{LN}(\tilde{x})W_Q,\ \mathrm{LN}(\tilde{x})W_K,\ \mathrm{LN}(\tilde{x})W_V\) \(e_{ij} \gets q_i^{\top}k_j + (q_i + v)^{\top}R_{i-j}\) \(e_{ij} \gets -\infty\) for \(j > i\) \(x' \gets \tilde{x} + \mathrm{softmax}(e/\sqrt{d_h})\,V\,W_O\) \(h \gets \mathrm{LN}(x')\) \([u, g] \gets \mathrm{Conv1d}_{d \to 2d}(h)\); \(\tilde{h} \gets u \odot \sigma(g)\) \(z \gets \mathrm{DepthwiseConv1d}_{K}(\tilde{h})\) \(c \gets \mathrm{Dropout}(\mathrm{Conv1d}_{d \to d}(\mathrm{Swish}(\mathrm{BN}(z))))\) \(x'' \gets x' + c\) \(x''\)

Implementation Mapping and Deviations

Table [tab:conformer-mapping] maps the paper block onto the toolkit. The substantive deviations are the two residual scalings and the second feed-forward layer: the paper keeps both \(\tfrac12\) Macaron coefficients and wraps \(\mathrm{FFN}_2\) in the block, whereas conformer uses full steps and returns the state after the convolution module, letting the outer HybridLayer apply its shared \(\mathrm{norm}_2 + \mathrm{FFN}\) (also at full step). The decomposition is deliberate—it keeps MoE routing, Mixture-of-Depths, mHC/Hyperloop streams, AttnRes, FlashNorm fusion, BitNet projections and the per-parameter-group optimizer routing available for the second FFN, none of which would survive a private FFN inside the mixer.

0.95L3.6cmL4.4cmX Paper component & Toolkit implementation & Notes
\(\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{FFN}_1\) (pre-norm) & private FFN inside ConformerAttention; Swish; full-step residual & conformer.macaron: true (default); the \(\tfrac12\) coefficient of the paper is dropped; disabling leaves attention \(+\) convolution only
MHSA, relative sinusoidal PE & own \(q/k/v/out\) projections; model-wide PE via conformer_use_pe (default true) & paper’s relative sinusoid \(\approx\) sinusoidal_rotary; no dedicated Transformer-XL module (RoPE is the model-wide default)
Convolution module & LN \(\to\) pointwise \(\to\) GLU \(\to\) depthwise \(\to\) BN \(\to\) Swish \(\to\) pointwise \(\to\) dropout & conformer.kernel_size (32), conformer.conv_norm (batch/group/layer)
\(\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{FFN}_2\) at half step & HybridLayer \(\mathrm{norm}_2 + \mathrm{FFN}\), full step & justified by Table 5 of : \(1.9/4.4\) vs. \(1.9/4.5\) dev WER (both coefficients dropped)
Final LayerNorm & HybridLayer final norm & unchanged from every other mixer

Dropout (\(p=0.1\)) & model.dims.dropout & global, per-block

Why the full-step FFN is safe.

Dropping the Macaron \(\tfrac12\) changes the per-branch residual scale, not the expressive form of the block: the full-step variant is exactly what ablate in their Table 5, where it moves dev-clean/dev-other WER from \(1.9/4.4\) (half step) to \(1.9/4.5\) (full step), i.e. one tenth of a point. The toolkit therefore uses full steps for both feed-forward layers; the first stays private to the mixer, and the second is the shared one, which preserves the composability described above.

Published Ablations

Table [tab:conformer-ablations] summarizes the ablations that motivate the default configuration. Values are the ones reported by ; the qualitative ordering is what the defaults encode.

Reuse of Existing Infrastructure

Because ConformerAttention returns a delta and inherits the mixer(config, pos_encoder=...) constructor, the entire stack is reused without special cases:

  • Model classes: text encoder (mlm/sbert/text_classification), causal decoder (causal_lm), Vision Transformer (patch_prediction/classification/segmentation) and frankenstein_audio (asr, audio_classification).

  • Normalization: all 6 variants, including partial RMSNorm and FlashNorm fusion on \(\mathrm{norm}_1\)/\(\mathrm{norm}_2\); the convolution module keeps its own BatchNorm unless conformer.conv_norm selects group or layer normalization.

  • Routing and residuals: MoE, Mixture-of-Depths, mHC, Hyperloop, AttnRes and the BitNet ternary projections (the private FFN and the convolution projections are BitLinear-aware).

  • Optimizers: all 23 families with per-group prefixes; mixer parameters, including the depthwise kernel and the convolution norms, route to the attention group.

  • KV cache: conformer is registered as not cacheable (supported=False), because the depthwise-convolution state and the BatchNorm running statistics would have to be carried across steps. generate() falls back to the full-recompute path, which is exact.

When to Use It

  • Speech: the default mixer for asr and audio_classification; at 40 ms frames after \(4\times\) subsampling the kernel of 32 spans \(\sim\)1.28 s of context, roughly the width of a phone sequence.

  • Text and vision: a strong drop-in for standard when the data has local structure (character-level models, code, OCR, patch sequences); it costs one depthwise convolution and two extra norms per layer over a plain attention block.

  • Streaming decoding: usable in mode: decoder with causal convolution padding, but without the incremental cache of Appendix 28; the depthwise recurrence is the missing piece.

Audio: Speech Recognition and Audio Classification

Executive Summary

frankenstein_audio is the fourth model class of the toolkit. It owns an audio frontend—log-mel filterbanks or a raw spectrogram, optional SpecAugment , and two stride-2 convolutions that reduce the frame rate by \(4\times\)—and then runs the same HybridLayer stack as the text encoder over the resulting frame sequence. Because the stack is modality-agnostic, every sequence mixer (including the Conformer of Appendix 30), normalization, residual strategy, positional encoding, optimizer and routing block is available unchanged. The class supports two tasks: automatic speech recognition (asr, with a CTC or an RNN-Transducer loss) and audio classification (audio_classification, clip-level cross-entropy). The same frontend, driven with audio.feature: raw, accepts multichannel one-dimensional sensor signals such as EEG, EMG or accelerometer traces for classification.

The reference recipe is the Conformer frontend of : 80-channel log-mel filterbanks with a 25 ms window and a 10 ms stride, two \(3\times3\) convolutions with stride 2, a linear projection to the model width, and SpecAugment with frequency width \(F=27\), ten time masks and a maximum time-mask ratio \(p_S = 0.05\). The three reference sizes (S/M/L) are reproduced in Table [tab:audio-sizes].

The frankenstein_audio Model Class

Audio Frontend

The frontend module turns a batch of waveforms \(w \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times T}\) (or a batch of multichannel clips \(w \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times C \times T}\) in raw mode) into a feature map:

  1. Framing: the waveform is cut into overlapping windows of window_ms \(=25\) ms every stride_ms \(=10\) ms, with a Hann window, at sample_rate \(=16000\) Hz. At the reference rate this yields frames of 400 samples with a 160-sample hop, i.e. 100 frames per second.

  2. Spectral representation (audio.feature):

    • logmel (default): an \(80\)-bin mel filterbank (Equation [eq:audio-mel]) followed by a log compression;

    • spectrogram: \(\log|\mathrm{STFT}(w)|^2\) with no mel projection;

    • raw: no spectral transform; the clip is fed as a \(C \times T\) map (Section 31.8).

  3. SpecAugment : \(F\) frequency channels are masked per clip, and up to time_masks time bands of width at most \(p_S \cdot T\) are masked, both with zero fill (training only).

The mel filterbank is \[M_k(f) = \max\Big(0,\ \min\Big(\tfrac{f-f_{k-1}}{f_k-f_{k-1}},\ \tfrac{f_{k+1}-f}{f_{k+1}-f_k}\Big)\Big), \label{eq:audio-filterbank}\] for \(K = 80\) triangular filters spaced on the mel scale, \(\mathrm{mel}(f) = 2595 \log_{10}(1 + f/700)\), and the log-mel feature is \[x_k = \log\Big(\sum_{f} M_k(f)\,|X(f)|^2 + \epsilon\Big). \label{eq:audio-mel}\] When torchaudio is importable, the frontend uses torchaudio.transforms.MelSpectrogram for Equation [eq:audio-mel]; otherwise it falls back to a pure-PyTorch implementation built on torch.stft and a cached filterbank matrix. The two paths are numerically equivalent up to filterbank convention (HTK vs. Slaney mel spacing), and the pure-PyTorch path is what keeps CPU-only CI free of the optional audio extra.

Convolutional Subsampling

Two convolutional stages reduce the frame rate by \(4\times\) (10 ms \(\to\) 40 ms), which is what makes a 30-second utterance a \(\sim\)750-token sequence instead of 3000: \[F = \mathrm{Dropout}\Big(W_p\,\mathrm{Conv2d}_{3\times3,\,s=2}\big(\mathrm{Conv2d}_{3\times3,\,s=2}(X)\big)\Big), \qquad W_p \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_c}, \label{eq:audio-subsampling}\] where \(X\) is the \(\texttt{n\_\allowbreak mels} \times T'\) feature map with conv_channels channels after the first stage, and \(W_p\) projects the flattened channels to the model width \(d\). Both stages are fixed at \(3\times3\) kernels with stride 2; audio.conv_channels (32) sets the channel width of the first stage and audio.n_fft (400) the STFT size.

Forced Encoder Mode and the HybridLayer Stack

frankenstein_audio forces mode: encoder, exactly as frankenstein_vit does: the audio tasks are bidirectional (a CTC or transducer encoder must see both past and future frames), and the Conformer’s convolution padding is symmetric in encoder mode. The class mirrors the ViT wrapper pattern—frontend, HybridLayer stack, task head—and its layer loop keeps the same hooks, so AttnRes, mHC, Hyperloop, looped depth, MoE, Mixture-of-Depths and BitNet all work without audio-specific code. All task heads are built after the final normalization:

  • CTC: \(\mathrm{Linear}(d, V+1)\) over the frame sequence, where the extra class is the blank.

  • RNN-T: a one-layer LSTM prediction network over the previous non-blank labels (audio.asr_decoder_dim, asr_decoder_layers, asr_decoder_dropout), and a joint network \(z_{t,u} = \tanh(W_e h_t + W_p h_u + b)\), \(\mathrm{logits}_{t,u} = W_o z_{t,u}\).

  • Classification: a pooled vector (global average pooling, or a learned [CLS] token prepended to the frame sequence, per pooling_mode) projected to num_classes logits.

Automatic Speech Recognition

CTC

Connectionist temporal classification marginalizes over all frame-level alignments that collapse to the target label sequence \(y\) under the many-to-one map \(\mathcal{B}\) (merge repeats, delete blanks): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{CTC}} = -\log \sum_{\pi \in \mathcal{B}^{-1}(y)} \prod_{t=1}^{T} p(\pi_t \mid x), \label{eq:audio-ctc}\] computed with torch.nn.functional.ctc_loss in log space with zero_infinity=False, so that impossible alignments do not poison the gradient.

RNN-Transducer

The RNN-T loss sums over label-and-blank alignments on the \(T \times (U+1)\) lattice. With \(\alpha_{t,u}\) the log-probability of the prefix \(y_{1:u}\) after \(t\) encoder frames, the forward recursion is \[\alpha_{t,u} = \operatorname{logsumexp}\Big( \underbrace{\alpha_{t-1,u} + \log p(\varnothing \mid t-1, u)}_{\text{advance time}}, \; \underbrace{\alpha_{t,u-1} + \log p(y_u \mid t, u-1)}_{\text{emit label}} \Big), \label{eq:audio-rnnt}\] with \(\alpha_{0,0} = 0\) and \(-\infty\) elsewhere, \(p(\cdot \mid t,u) = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathrm{logits}_{t,u})\), and \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{RNN-T}} = -\alpha_{T,U}. \label{eq:audio-rnnt-loss}\] The implementation is autograd-friendly in pure PyTorch (log-domain dynamic programming on the lattice, with the gradient obtained by the standard backward recursion), and takes the torchaudio.functional.rnnt_loss fast path when the optional dependency is installed. The lattice is \(O(T \cdot U)\) in memory, which is why the predictor is kept shallow (audio.asr_decoder_layers, default 1) and narrow (audio.asr_decoder_dim, default 320). The loss is selected with audio.asr_loss (ctc by default).

Decoding and Error Rate

Greedy CTC decoding takes the per-frame argmax, collapses repeats and removes blanks. Greedy RNN-T decoding alternates a label emission with a frame advance until the blank is scored higher than the next label. Both are scored with the character error rate \[\mathrm{CER} = \frac{S + D + I}{N}, \label{eq:audio-cer}\] where \(S\), \(D\), \(I\) are the substitutions, deletions and insertions of the Levenshtein alignment against the reference transcript and \(N\) is the reference length.

Audio Classification

Classification reuses the pooling and head conventions of the Vision Transformer (Appendix 24): pooling_mode: cls prepends a learned token and reads position 0, pooling_mode: gap (the default) averages the frame outputs. The head is a zero-initialized \(\mathrm{Linear}(d, K)\) trained with cross-entropy and the same label smoothing knob as the vision tasks. SpecAugment applies to the feature map before subsampling, so it augments the input, never the token sequence.

SpecAugment

Following in its “LibriSpeech basic” configuration, the two mask types are applied independently per clip: \[\Delta f \sim \mathcal{U}[0, F], \quad f_0 \sim \mathcal{U}[0, \nu - \Delta f], \qquad \Delta t \sim \mathcal{U}[0, p_S \cdot T], \quad t_0 \sim \mathcal{U}[0, T - \Delta t], \label{eq:audio-specaugment}\] with \(F = 27\), time_masks \(= 10\) and \(p_S = 0.05\), each mask zeroing a \(\Delta f \times \Delta t\) rectangle. Time warping, the third SpecAugment transform, is not implemented—it requires a per-sample warp of the time axis that interacts poorly with the fixed-length bucketing of the dataset. Frequency and time masking carry most of the regularization benefit in the paper’s own ablations, and both are disabled at evaluation time.

Example Configurations

The ASR examples use astroza/chilean-jokes-festival-de-vina (Spanish audio at 16 kHz with transcripts, 50 rows), a dataset small enough to run end-to-end on CPU as a smoke test. The classification example falls back to the synthetic DummyAudioDataset when no dataset is reachable.

model_class: frankenstein_audio
model:
  dims: {hidden_size: 144, num_layers: 16, num_heads: 4}
  dims.layer_pattern: [conformer, ...]   # 16 entries
  attention.conformer: {kernel_size: 32, macaron: true, conv_norm: batch}
audio:
  feature: logmel
  sample_rate: 16000
  n_mels: 80
  window_ms: 25
  stride_ms: 10
  n_fft: 400
  conv_channels: 32
  asr_loss: ctc          # or transducer
  asr_decoder_dim: 320
  asr_decoder_layers: 1
  asr_decoder_dropout: 0.1
  spec_augment: {enabled: true, freq_mask_width: 27,
                 time_masks: 10, time_mask_ratio: 0.05}
audio_dataset:
  dataset_name: astroza/chilean-jokes-festival-de-vina
  split: test
  audio_column: audio
  text_column: text
training:
  task: asr
  asr: {loss: ctc}       # optional override of audio.asr_loss

SpecAugment is part of the acoustic frontend (“audio.spec_augment”), so it is applied to the feature map before subsampling and is active only in training mode. The optional training.asr.loss block overrides audio.asr_loss for presets that want to switch between CTC and RNN-T without editing the architecture block; the two must agree because the transducer head is built from the model-side knob.

Generic 1-D Signals: EEG and Beyond

The frontend is not tied to speech. With audio.feature: raw, the mel filterbank and SpecAugment are skipped and the clip is treated as a multichannel \(C \times T\) map, with audio.in_channels: C. The two stride-2 convolutions then act as a learned filter bank over time (and, as a side effect, over the channel axis), the linear projection produces \(d\)-wide tokens, and the HybridLayer stack sees a sequence of frames exactly as it does for speech. This makes the class usable, at least for classification, on:

  • EEG: \(C\) electrodes \(\times\) \(T\) samples per epoch, labelled with a cognitive state, sleep stage or pathology; electrodes play the role of the mel channels.

  • EMG / ECG / EDA: one or a few channels, labelled with gesture, activity or anomaly class.

  • Accelerometer / IMU: \(C \in \{3, 6, 9\}\) axes, labelled with activity or device state.

  • Industrial and environmental sensors: vibration, pressure, acoustic emission traces, labelled per window.

What carries over.

Everything downstream of the frontend: all 45 mixers (Conformer is a good default because its convolution branch matches the local morphology of biosignals), all 6 norms, AttnRes/mHC/MoE/MoD, the 23 optimizers, the frozen-encoder text_classification recipe, and the checkpoint/deployment paths. Length bucketing, padding masks and the CER/CER-style evaluation are dataset-side and are unaffected by the modality.

Limitations.

Raw mode is a convenience, not a replacement for a domain frontend:

  1. Channel axis downsampling. The two stride-2 Conv2d stages are fixed and halve both spatial axes, so a montage with fewer than four channels loses its channel axis entirely; keep \(C \geq 4\) (or project the montage to a wider map first).

  2. No montage geometry. Electrode positions, referential vs. bipolar montages and inter-channel correlations are not encoded; the convolution sees channels as an unordered stack, unlike EEG-specific models with topographic or graph priors.

  3. No spectral prior. logmel and spectrogram assume audio band limits and mel spacing that do not apply below 20 Hz or above 8 kHz; raw mode avoids the mismatch but also loses the band-aligned inductive bias.

  4. Classification only. CTC and RNN-T require a token-level target sequence. Sequence-to-sequence labelling of sensor windows (e.g. sleep-stage sequences) is out of scope; use per-window classification and a post-hoc decoder instead.

  5. Statistics and normalization. The convolution module’s BatchNorm uses per-batch statistics; for EEG the amplitude scale varies by subject and session, so per-channel normalization in the dataset is recommended over relying on the frontend.

  6. Sampling-rate assumptions. sample_rate is used to convert window_ms/stride_ms into samples; for raw signals set it to the true acquisition rate and choose the window in milliseconds accordingly.

PyTorch Pseudocode

Input: waveforms \(w\), lengths \(\ell\), transcripts \(y\) (ASR) or labels \(c\) (classification) \(F \gets \texttt{frontend}(w)\) \(F \gets \texttt{spec\_\allowbreak augment}(F)\) \(F \gets \texttt{conv2d}_{3\times3, s=2}(F)\); \(F \gets \texttt{conv2d}_{3\times3, s=2}(F)\) \(x \gets \texttt{dropout}(\texttt{linear}(F))\) \(x \gets x + \texttt{pos\_\allowbreak encoder}(x)\) \(x \gets \texttt{layer}(x)\) \(x \gets \texttt{final\_\allowbreak norm}(x)\) \(\mathrm{logits} \gets \texttt{ctc\_\allowbreak head}(x)\); \(\mathcal{L} \gets \texttt{ctc\_\allowbreak loss}(\log\mathrm{softmax}(\mathrm{logits}), y, \ell/4)\) \(h^{pred} \gets \texttt{predictor}(y)\); \(\mathrm{logits}_{t,u} \gets \texttt{joint}(x_t, h^{pred}_u)\) \(\mathcal{L} \gets \texttt{rnnt\_\allowbreak loss}(\mathrm{logits}, y, \ell/4)\) \(\mathrm{logits} \gets \texttt{class\_\allowbreak head}(\texttt{pool}(x))\); \(\mathcal{L} \gets \mathrm{CE}(\mathrm{logits}, c)\)

Deviations and Implementation Notes

  • Optional torchaudio. The frontend prefers torchaudio.transforms but never requires it; the pure-PyTorch fallback keeps the CPU CI and the cpu extra torchaudio-free (decision D7 of the architecture guide).

  • Time warping. Not implemented (Equation [eq:audio-specaugment] covers frequency and time masking only); time warping is the transform the paper uses least.

  • Shallow predictor. The RNN-T prediction network is a single LSTM layer by default (audio.asr_decoder_layers), trading the paper’s deeper predictor for an \(O(T \cdot U)\) lattice that fits in memory at the reference batch sizes.

  • Export. The HuggingFace and GGUF exports reject audio artifacts explicitly, as they do for SBERT: there is no upstream FrankensteinForAudioClassification mapping. deploy –format standard|quantized works unchanged.

  • Cache. There is no incremental encoder cache for audio; ASR consumes a whole utterance per forward.

Dynamic Token Embeddings (EELBERT)

Executive Summary

embedding.dynamic replaces the trainable \(V\times H\) input embedding table with an on-the-fly \(n\)-gram pooling hash of the token string, following EELBERT . The lookup table disappears from the parameter count, from checkpoints and from native deployment artifacts. The effect is largest in the small models where the lookup layer dominates the budget—in BERT-tiny the input embedding accounts for roughly \(90\%\) of the parameters—and it is complementary to quantization, pruning and distillation.

Dynamic embeddings are frozen: they are never trained and never receive gradients. They only change how a token id becomes a vector; everything downstream (mixers, normalization, residuals, routing, optimizers) is unchanged. As in the paper, the output head remains an independent, untied matrix: during masked-LM pre-training it still stores a \(V\times H\) matrix, so the size advantage materialises in the backbone-only or post-fine-tuning artifact (the training checkpoint is not automatically \(15\times\) smaller). The implementation lives in , the configuration contract is the model.embedding.dynamic.* block, and the tokenizer vocabulary is injected by the training, deployment and inference pipelines through .

Algorithm

Let \(w\) be a token string of \(l\) bytes with byte values \(b_1,\dots,b_l\), and let \(d=H\) be the embedding width. The algorithm has five steps, with \(N\) the maximum \(n\)-gram size and \(B\) the hash bucket.

  1. Seeds. Draw \(d\) seeds from a single stored random state \(s\), \[\mathbf{h} = (h_1,\dots,h_d) \in \{0,\dots,B-1\}^d, \qquad \mathbf{h} \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(\text{seed}=s).\] Only the integer \(s\) is persisted; the seed vector is a deterministic function of it.

  2. \(i\)-gram signatures. For \(i=1,\dots,N\) compute the polynomial rolling hash of every \(i\)-gram, \[\sigma_i(j) = \Big(\sum_{t=0}^{i-1} b_{j+t}\,a^{\,i-1-t}\Big) \bmod B, \qquad j=1,\dots,k_i, \qquad k_i=\max(l-i+1,0),\] with \(a=257\) (prime, larger than any UTF-8 byte). The hashes are computed incrementally: the \((i{+}1)\)-gram hash reuses the \(i\)-gram hash and appends one byte, so the whole token costs \(\mathcal{O}(lN)\) integer operations.

  3. Partitioned projection. Split \(\mathbf{h}\) into \(N\) contiguous parts \(\mathbf{h}_i\) of length \(d_i\) with \[\sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i = d, \qquad d_i \propto i,\] so longer \(n\)-grams receive more dimensions. The projection matrix of each gram size is the outer product \[\mathbf{P}_i = \sigma_i \otimes \mathbf{h}_i \in \mathbb{Z}^{k_i\times d_i}.\]

  4. Folding. Map each entry into \([-1,1]\) through \[\phi(x) = \frac{(x \bmod B) - \mathbf{1}[x \bmod B > B/2]\;B}{B/2} \in (-1, 1],\] which keeps the embedding bounded without storing or normalising a table.

  5. Pooling and concatenation. Average each projection across its \(k_i\) rows and concatenate the \(N\) pieces: \[\mathbf{e}_i = \frac{1}{k_i}\sum_{j=1}^{k_i} \phi\big(\mathbf{P}_i[j,:]\big), \qquad \mathbf{e} = [\mathbf{e}_1;\dots;\mathbf{e}_N] \in \mathbb{R}^{d}.\] When a token is shorter than \(i\), \(k_i=0\) and that partition contributes a zero vector.

Because the hash is polynomial over characters, morphologically related tokens (e.g. runner and running) share many \(1\)/\(2\)/\(3\)-grams and land close in embedding space. The paper shows this matters most for small models: replacing the \(n\)-gram hash with a purely random (position-preserving) hash costs \(5.0\) GLUE points for BERT-mini but only \(0.3\) for BERT-base.

Configuration Contract

Dynamic-embedding configuration. The block composes with embedding.conv.*, which applies a Conv1d over the \(H\)-wide dynamic stream.
Key (model.embedding.dynamic.*) Default Effect
enabled false Replace the input lookup table with the frozen hash embedding. Mutually exclusive with embedding.factorized.enabled.
ngram_max 3 Maximum \(n\)-gram size \(N\); must satisfy \(1 \le N \le H\).
bucket 1000000007 Hash bucket \(B\) (\(10^9+7\) in the paper). Changing it changes every embedding.
seed 42 Random state \(s\) for the seeds; identical seeds reproduce identical embeddings.
precompute true Memoise the \(V\times H\) table in a non-persistent buffer (pure caching; never saved or exported).

The schema enforces the mutual exclusion with factorized embeddings twice: a conditional if/then rule in src/schema/_conditional_rules.yaml and a __post_init__ check in FrankensteinModelConfig. The block is only valid for the text classes (frankenstein_text_encoder and frankenstein_text_decoder); the ViT uses a convolutional patch embedding and the audio frontend is not a vocabulary lookup, so config_loader rejects the combination for those classes.

Vocabulary Injection and Lifecycle

Hash embeddings consume token strings, while models receive integer ids. The configuration therefore carries a runtime-only, non-schema field token_vocab (id-ordered token strings). inject_token_vocab(config, tokenizer) extracts it from a HuggingFace tokenizer (get_vocab()) or from the legacy SentencePiece wrapper (vocab, token \(\to\) id), attaches it before build_model, and aligns vocab_size with the tokenizer ids. The training engine ( and ), deployment checkpoint loader and inference engine all call the helper, so the vocabulary need not appear in the YAML. Constructing DynamicEmbedding without a vocabulary raises an actionable error.

The checkpoint stores no embedding weights: state_dict() contains nothing for the input layer, and the vocabulary travels with the tokenizer saved next to the checkpoint. With precompute: true the computed table is a non-persistent buffer—it follows .to(device) but is excluded from checkpoints and exports, so it is exactly equivalent to the on-the-fly computation. With precompute: false the hash is recomputed per batch (lower resident memory, slower steps); the two paths agree up to float32 reduction order.

The native deployment artifacts and the GGUF exporter therefore keep the size benefit. The HuggingFace Transformers export cannot run the custom hash, so it materialises the computed table as a frozen nn.Embedding, records the conversion in the compatibility report and emits a warning that the EELBERT size advantage is not preserved in that artifact.

Size Accounting and Paper Results

The removed block is \(V\times H\) weights; the added block is only the optional Conv1d (\(k H^2 + H\)) when embedding.conv.enabled is true. In our preset (BERT-tiny geometry: 2 layers, \(H=128\), 2 heads, FFN reduced to \(128\), \(V=30{,}522\)), the input table removes \(3.91\)M weights while the untied MLM head keeps \(3.94\)M, leaving \(4.15\)M total parameters—the paper’s own accounting, where the head is dropped only for deployment.

Table 16 summarises the reference results reported by .

The complexity of a token embedding is \(\mathcal{O}(l\,d)\) against the \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) table lookup of BERT: for the 128–768 widths used by BERT the additional latency is negligible at the base scale but becomes visible on tiny models (about \(2.3\times\) for EELBERT-tiny in the table). The paper proposes three mitigations that this implementation leaves as engineering options: a sparse fixed-width mask on the outer product (\(\mathcal{O}(l\,s)\) with \(s\ll d\)), parallel per-token hashing, and a bounded cache of the most frequent \(n\)-grams.

Implementation Map

  • — DynamicEmbedding: seeds, chunked rolling hash, partitioned outer product, folding, pooling, optional Conv1d, embedding_table().

  • — emb dispatch (dynamic \(\to\) factorized \(\to\) nn.Embedding); the decoder reuses it through its encoder backbone. Mutual exclusion and range checks live in .

  • — token_strings() and inject_token_vocab(), shared by the engine, the CLI training path, deployment and inference.

  • — frozen-table materialisation and the export warning.

  • — determinism per seed, \([-1,1]\) bounds, morphology similarity, precompute vs. on-the-fly parity, zero trainable parameters, vocabulary and configuration errors, encoder/decoder forwards, schema rule and export materialisation.

  • and — presets; both are smoke-tested, and the E2E harness covers the combination as trans_dynamic_emb.

Scope and Limitations

Dynamic embeddings are a compression mechanism, not a new representation-learning objective: they do not approximate a trained BERT embedding, and they cannot be trained or fine-tuned themselves. Because the mapping is a deterministic function of (string, seed, \(B\), \(N\)), changing any of those invalidates previously trained checkpoints. The design also couples the model to the tokenizer that produced the training ids: the vocabulary (and therefore the token strings) is part of the artifact contract, and a tokenizer swap silently changes every input embedding. Finally, the HuggingFace export loses the size advantage by construction, so on-device deployments should prefer the native checkpoint, the deployment package or GGUF.

The Experiment Harness

This annex documents the machinery behind Section 9. Its purpose is reproducibility across rounds: an experiment is simply a new folder under experimentos/, and the same consolidation, reporting, and publishing scripts operate on it unchanged. The harness is deliberately decoupled from the model code in both directions—it only reads what training and deployment write—so an experiment never depends on the library version that produced it, and the library never learns about the campaign that used it. The practical consequence is that rounds remain interpretable and rebuildable long after the library has evolved.

Stages and Records

Each configuration is one YAML file and one slug. The slug is a short identifier that encodes the family and the mixers: attn_nsa__engram is a hybrid pair (first mixer nsa, second mixer engram), attn_single_mamba is a single-mixer baseline, and the ablation families carry their own prefixes (opt_, norm_, pe_, trans_, vit_, task_, tokenizer_, batch_, realdata_, audio_, bitnet_). Every run executes the same five stages: train, export the checkpoint, deploy in a standard and a quantized format, evaluate four held-out masked prompts per format, and export the Hugging Face package.

The failure policy deserves a note. A failure in one stage is recorded, does not abort the sweep, and surfaces later as a missing row rather than as a silent zero. The distinction matters for downstream statistics: a model that failed to train must not be mistaken for a model that trained and scored zero, and a missing cell in the atlas must be traceable to a recorded failure rather than to an unnoticed gap.

Three recorders write independently and are joined only at reporting time:

  1. The per-step training log. One CSV per run with one row per optimisation step: loss, accuracy, learning rate, gradient norms per parameter group, clipping ratio, step time and throughput. Round 2 logged 2,656,372 rows, which are streamed and reduced to per-epoch means before any chart is drawn—no one plots 2.6 million points, and the reduction is deterministic, so the published curve is an exact function of the raw log.

  2. The parameter census. For every configuration, the number of parameters in each module group (attention, embeddings, FFN, head, normalization, positional encoding, mHC, router, residual). This is what separates “the model is bigger” from “the attention block is bigger”, and it allows cost to be attributed per component rather than per model.

  3. The pipeline ledger. One row per stage execution with category, status, duration and return code. It is the only record of the failures, and therefore the only source for the reliability analysis.

The Stage Ledger of Round 2

Table 17 reproduces the ledger. Training dominates both the record count and the cost: 1,039 attempts, of which 868 succeeded and 171 failed, with a median of 68 minutes and a P90 of 84 minutes per attempt—906 CPU-hours in total, of which 905 belong to the 868 analysed runs and the remainder to the discarded attempts. Every other stage is measured in seconds. Deployment is the only stage besides training that fails (104 times out of 1,734), and the failures are symmetric: whenever a configuration’s standard export fails, its quantized export fails too. The symmetry points to a shared root cause upstream of quantization—checkpoint or configuration serialisation—rather than to the quantization step itself. Evaluation and Hugging Face export never failed in the analysed population.

The 275 failures are informative rather than merely inconvenient. All 171 training failures sit outside the 868 analysed configurations, which were selected precisely because they trained; the 104 deployment failures occur in symmetric pairs, as explained above. Read as a reliability measurement, the ledger says that the pipeline fails loudly and early—in training or in export—and never silently during evaluation. The failure distribution by family, and the identical-fingerprint analysis of the four mixers that collapse at 32 tokens, are charted in Appendix 34.

Consolidated Datasets

The reporting chain starts from the raw per-run folders and produces a small set of joined tables (Table [tab:round-datasets]). The join key is the configuration slug: master.csv carries one row per configuration with the parameter census, the training summary, the stage statuses, and the inference scores attached side by side. The tables are published with the report so that any figure can be rebuilt from them without the 702 MB of per-step logs, and the raw per-run CSVs are published separately, gzip-compressed, for anyone who needs step-level data.

Rebuilding a Round

The pipeline is three scripts and a publisher, all standard-library or pandas/numpy/matplotlib only, and every step runs on CPU:

  1. python experimentos/to_csv.py N reads experimentos/N/ without modifying it and writes consolidated CSVs to experimentos/N/csvs/: the inference table with the notes column expanded into one column per key=value pair, the parameter census as one row per configuration, the results ledger as a flat table, and the per-run training CSVs concatenated together with their per-run mean, standard deviation and final row.

  2. python experimentos/N/report/build_data.py streams the raw logs, joins the three recorders by slug and writes master.csv and the derived tables.

  3. python experimentos/N/report/make_charts.py renders every figure twice (dark and light themes) and records the captions in registry.json; make_report.py consumes both to emit the bilingual static page.

  4. bash experimentos/N/report/publish.sh copies the page, the figures and the datasets to the GitHub Pages mirror. It never commits or pushes by itself.

The paper figures are a curated subset of the same chart builders, exported as vector PDFs by make_paper_figures.py. The division of labour is deliberate: one set of chart builders feeds both the web report and the paper, so a number in the paper and the corresponding pixel on the website cannot drift apart. The whole chain is CPU-only and reproduces every number in this annex from the published datasets.

Round 1: The Pilot

Round 1 exercised the same harness end-to-end at smoke scale: 5,129 stage records, training runs of roughly half a minute, and the same five-stage sequence. Its purpose was to validate the mechanics—slug generation, ledger bookkeeping, deployment symmetry and the reporting joins—before committing CPU time to the real campaign. It is not analysed further here because the runs were too short to separate architectures; its value is procedural: Round 2 inherited a harness whose bookkeeping had already been exercised and whose failure modes were already known.

Round 2: The Mixer Atlas

This annex reports Round 2 in full. It follows the order of the published report: the parameter landscape, the training outcomes, the learning dynamics, the A\(\times\)B atlas, the ablation sweeps, the deployment and inference measurements, the reliability of the pipeline, and the correlations between the measured features. All numbers come from master.csv of the published dataset; all figures are regenerated by make_paper_figures.py from the same chart builders as the web report, so the annex and the website cannot disagree.

Setup

The population is 868 configurations: 703 hybrid-pair records (667 unique pairs after collapsing the retnet_attn alias duplicate), 38 single-mixer baselines, 48 vision transformers and 79 ablations. Every run trains for 100 epochs (about 3,000 steps) on a 512-token Spanish vocabulary with 32-token sequences, one seed, the same warm-up-plus-cosine schedule and BitNet enabled by default. Holding the schedule, the data and the budget fixed is what makes the cells comparable: the only moving parts are the architectural choices under study. Hybrid pairs are the two-element combinations of the 42-entry mixer list, with layer 0 running mixer A and layer 1 running mixer B; no reversed pair exists, so the first/second asymmetry is descriptive. A cell of the grid is covered only if both of its mixers train in every configuration that contains them: the grid has \(42\times41/2 = 861\) cells and 667 were measured.

The Parameter Landscape

The 868 configurations span 127,328 to 415,904 parameters, with a median of 220,160. Hybrid pairs sit in the middle of the range because they stack two attention modules; the smallest runs are single-mixer baselines such as attn_single_mamba (127,328 parameters), and the largest is engram__conformer at 415,904, driven by the engram memory bank, which attaches a large key–value table to the attention block.

The composition chart (Figure 87) is the most useful diagnostic of the section. The token embeddings and the output head are fixed costs of roughly 49k parameters each, so almost every difference between configurations is paid in the attention block and the FFN—the two components the experiments actually vary. Vision transformers are the most parameter-hungry family because they add patch embeddings and a larger classification head, while the optimizer, normalization and positional-encoding ablations keep the same 210k backbone by design, so that only the ablated component differs. Parameter cost has a clear per-mixer reading: engram adds 100k–160k parameters wherever it appears, and mamba and retnet are among the cheapest second mixers even though they are the worst performers—cheap and bad, the worst combination on both axes.

Training Outcomes

Across the hybrid pairs, the final training loss ranges from 8.116 to 10.450 nats (median 9.595). The best pair is nsa__engram at 8.116, followed by gated_deltanet2__sparda (8.567) and falcon3__conformer (8.620); the worst, gqa__tucker, needs 10.450. The spread between the best and worst pair is wider than the spread between almost all optimizer ablations—the strongest argument in the round for choosing the attention pair deliberately: the mixer stack matters more than the optimizer.

Loss and held-out accuracy, however, disagree. Their rank correlation over the pairs is weak; the pair with the absolute best loss scores 0.0% top-1, while the best-accuracy pair (fox__falcon1a) reaches 12.55% with a worse training loss (9.292). The reason is resolution: with four evaluation sentences, a single lucky or unlucky token rewrites the ranking. Both signals are therefore reported throughout, and the inference tables should be read as a catastrophic-failure check rather than as a leaderboard. Table 18 lists the ten best pairs by final loss and Table 19 the ten best by held-out accuracy; the two tables have no pair in common.

Training Dynamics

Every run uses the same warm-up-plus-cosine schedule, so the learning curves are directly comparable without re-normalisation. The pair population is still descending at epoch 100: the median loss falls from about 10.2 nats at epoch 0 to 9.49 at the end. The sweep therefore measures speed of learning, not converged quality, and every ranking in this annex should be read as “which pair learns fastest in 3,000 steps” rather than “which pair is best in the limit”.

The optimisation statistics are calm. Gradient norms are stable across families (1.87 for the attention block, 0.92 for the FFN, 3.47 for the head), and the median clip ratio sits at 0.90—below the clipping threshold of 1.0—so most steps pass unclipped and clipping only fires on spikes. The throughput median is 357 tokens/s for the pair population; the 3k–31k tail visible in the charts belongs to the tokenizer and audio ablations, whose step timer covers only part of the work, which is why the Pareto analysis excludes it.

The A\(\times\)B Atlas

The atlas (Figure 95) is the centrepiece of the experiment: a matrix in which each cell is one hybrid pair, rows index the first mixer, columns index the second, and colour encodes the final loss. It is read in two directions. Column by column—fix the second mixer, vary the first—the second mixer dominates: a good B (sparsek, engram, mlra) keeps almost every A in the 8.9–9.6 nat band, while a bad B (mamba, retnet, bigbird) drags even the best A above 10 nats. Row by row—fix the first mixer, vary the second—no A rescues a bad B. The asymmetry is the visual form of the first finding of Section 9.

Coverage is almost complete: 667 of the 861 possible pairs were trained. The 158 pairs that never trained are exactly those containing cca, ccgqa, msa or ssog—four mixers that fail in every configuration—which accounts for the count: \(4\times41 - \binom{4}{2} = 158\).

Table 20 ranks second mixers by mean final loss across every pair that contains them. The Pairs column is the sample size behind each mean and should be read alongside it: a single-pair mean (for example mamba, with one pair) is anecdotal, while a 30–40 pair mean is a solid estimate. The bottom half of the table is as informative as the top: mamba, bigbird, longformer and retnet are cheap but consistently drag their pairs down—exactly the pattern the heatmaps show, and a warning against equating parameter economy with quality.

Interaction beats marginals.

Ranking mixers individually cannot reconstruct the atlas, because pairs interact. The synergy chart quantifies this: for each pair it measures how much better (or worse) the pair is than the average of its two marginal means, \[S_{A,B} = \frac{\mu_A + \mu_B}{2} - L_{A,B},\] where \(\mu_A\) and \(\mu_B\) are the mean losses of all pairs containing A and B respectively. Positive synergy means the pair beats what its parts would predict. nsa+engram gains 1.304 nats, and the top of the table shares a pattern: a cheap, clean first mixer stacked under a memory-heavy second one. The negative tail is dominated by gta, gqa and tucker as B—mixers that look average in isolation but clash when stacked after a strong A. For synthesis purposes the message is that a ranked list of mixers is a necessary summary but an insufficient design tool: the atlas, or at least the synergy table, must be consulted before composing a stack.

Ablations

Optimizers.

The optimizer sweep is the most sobering chart of the round: 23 optimizers, the same 210k backbone, and a final-loss range of only 10.10–10.77 nats (Table 22). q_apollo wins at 10.098 and galore_adamw closes the table at 10.772, but a dozen optimizers land on exactly 10.404—the run is too short for the choice of optimizer to separate from noise, and the honest summary at this budget is that most modern optimizers are interchangeable. The speed differences are real, however: mean step time varies by roughly 30%, and the second-order and orthogonalised methods (shampoo, muon) pay a visible overhead. When runs are short, the optimizer is best chosen for speed rather than for final loss.

Normalization and positional encoding.

Among the normalizations (Table 23), flash_norm wins clearly at 9.749 nats—half a nat ahead of the runner-up, a large margin by the standards of this round—while prms_norm and rms_norm lag. In the positional encodings (Table 24), the PAPE family (pape_ri, pape, pape_efficient) sweeps the podium, and classical RoPE is mid-table. Both results are useful calibration: “modern” is not automatically better on a 100-epoch run at this scale, and component choices that look like refinements in the literature can separate by half a nat here.

Structural switches.

The structural toggles (Table 25) separate more than the optimizers do—evidence that, at this scale, architecture is a stronger lever than the update rule. The three wins are factorised embeddings (9.623), a SwiGLU FFN (9.901) and two Hyperloop loops (9.908). The BitNet toggles land at 10.016, mHC at 10.186, and the residual variants between 10.43 and 10.49. Mixture-of-Depths is the worst switch at 10.854, consistent with its documented incompatibility with mHC at this depth.

Vision and tasks.

The vision block works. Segmentation reaches 90.7% mean held-out accuracy, classification 75.8% and patch prediction 69.9%. These scores are an order of magnitude above the MLM pairs (4.0% median) because the task is easier, not because the mixer matters more; the report therefore keeps the families separate and draws no cross-family conclusion. The tokenizer and task ablations behave as expected and mainly serve as scale anchors: the tokenizer moves the loss by several nats because it changes the vocabulary and the average sequence length, and the task changes it because the objective itself changes. Neither is comparable with the mixer sweep, and both are excluded from it.

Deployment and Inference

Post-training quantization is the good news of the round. Across the 810 configurations with both formats, mean top-1 moves from 5.62% to 5.43% and mean top-5 from 13.36% to 13.24%—deltas of \(-0.19\) and \(-0.12\) percentage points. Eight hundred of the 810 configurations are exactly unchanged, and the few that move do so by a single sample out of four. For a smoke-scale model this is the expected result, but it is worth measuring rather than assuming.

The speed story is less flattering, and the reason is structural. The quantized deployment is faster than the standard one in only 32.3% of runs (median ratio 0.64\(\times\)) because the deploy stage is dominated by serialisation and format conversion, not by inference; the evaluation stage, which does measure inference, is faster 51.2% of the time with a median 1.03\(\times\) speed-up. Inference itself takes about 10.5 s for four sentences—the number that matters at serving time.

The best inference configuration is not the best-loss configuration. mamba__engram hits three of four tokens in the top-5 (75.0%) with a training loss of 10.277, above the pair median. With four samples per configuration, top-5 is a blunt instrument: use it to catch catastrophic failures, not to crown a winner.

Reliability of the Pipeline

The ledger records 5,271 stage executions. 868 training runs succeeded and 171 failed with a non-zero exit code—all of them outside the 868 analysed configurations, which were selected precisely because they trained. Deployment failed 104 times out of 1,734, always in symmetric pairs: a configuration that fails the standard export also fails the quantized one, which points to a shared root cause (checkpoint or configuration serialisation) rather than to quantization itself.

Two data-quality findings shape the interpretation of the atlas. First, four mixers never train: cca, ccgqa, msa and ssog fail in their four singles and in all 158 pairs that contain them—exactly the 158 missing cells. Second, four mixers are indistinguishable at a 32-token context: standard, bigbird, longformer and titan share bit-identical losses and parameter counts because their windows (at least 64 tokens) cover the whole sequence and the position-augmented variant reduces to plain multi-head attention; they agree on all 33 shared second mixers. Separately, 37 pairs appear as attn_retnet__X and attn_retnet__X with identical metrics—two names for one implementation—which the atlas collapses to one row. Each of these facts is a caveat carried forward rather than a defect hidden: the atlas has 667 measured cells, 158 structurally missing ones, and four mixers that are, at this context length, the same model.

What Predicts Quality

Over the hybrid pairs, parameter count correlates with final loss at \(r = -0.20\) and with held-out accuracy at \(r = -0.07\): size barely buys quality here. What it does predict reliably is cost (\(r = 0.68\) with step time, \(r = 0.65\) with wall-clock). Training loss carries only a weak signal about inference quality (\(r = 0.14\) with top-5)—the quantitative form of the loss/accuracy disagreement noted above. Gradient norm and clip ratio are exactly redundant with each other (\(r = 1.00\)), which is expected because the clip ratio is computed from the gradient norm, and neither correlates with quality.

The correlation matrix of Figure 114 is computed over all 868 rows. Read that way, parameter count correlates with loss at \(-0.43\) and with accuracy at \(+0.42\), apparently contradicting the pair-only numbers. Both readings are correct, and the reconciliation is a textbook confound: the all-rows matrix is dominated by the contrast between vision transformers (larger, much lower loss, much higher accuracy) and MLM pairs, so it measures the gap between families rather than the effect of size within a family. Within the population the atlas is about—the hybrid pairs—size is close to irrelevant, and that is the number to quote.

Practical Reading and Next Steps

If a pair must be chosen blind, the round supports a simple heuristic: pick a memory-heavy second mixer (engram, sparsek, mlra) and a cheap, stable first mixer (fox, gqa, gated_deltanet2), and avoid mamba, retnet and bigbird as B. Expect about \(\pm0.3\) nats of interaction noise—larger than the difference between most optimizers, and therefore the dominant uncertainty when composing a stack.

The round also defines its own successor, and its limitations are the specification. The atlas should be re-run at 256–512 tokens, where the four window-collapsing mixers become distinguishable and the sparse patterns actually sparsify; the evaluation should use a 200-sentence held-out set scored by per-token log-likelihood, because four sentences cannot rank 800 configurations; the top pairs should train to 300 epochs, because every curve is still descending; the retnet alias and the four failing mixers should be fixed or removed from the list; and the ablation families should run at least three seeds, because their current spread is within seed noise. Finally, quantization should become the default deployment format: it cost 0.12 points of top-5 and sped up evaluation in half the runs.
